plan.title: Key statutes: SOX, RICO, FCA, FCPA

body.p: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognized when it is earned and expenses when incurred — not when cash moves. Almost all financial-statement fraud lives in that timing gap. Keep the equation in mind: Assets = Liabilities + Owners' equity; every fraudulent entry must still balance, which is why fraudsters force offsets somewhere.

FSF is the deliberate misrepresentation of a company's financial condition through intentional misstatement or omission to deceive users. It is the least frequent but most costly occupational-fraud category. It crosses from 'aggressive accounting' into fraud when there is a material misstatement plus intent to deceive users who rely on the statements.

body.h: Why it happens & how it's detected

ul: Motive: hit earnings/analyst targets, trigger bonuses, prop up a share price, or hide a decline.
Vertical (common-size) analysis — each line as a % of a base (sales for P&L, total assets for balance sheet). Best for spotting an abnormal COGS-to-sales or margin shift.
Horizontal analysis — % change line-by-line across periods.
Ratio analysis — receivable/inventory turnover, current ratio, gross margin.

body.key: Capitalizing a routine expense (booking a repair as a fixed asset) overstates assets AND overstates net income, because the expense is improperly deferred off the income statement. This exact mechanic is tested repeatedly.

body.p: Revenue growing faster than operating cash flow; receivables growing faster than sales; recurring 'one-time' items; a dominant CEO/CFO who overrides controls. (Stable operating cash flow funding dividends is a sign of health, not a red flag — a classic EXCEPT trap.)

body.case: Telecom — capacity swaps: two carriers sell each other equal network capacity at inflated prices, each booking the inflow as revenue while burying the outflow as a capital asset. Result: fictitious revenue + capitalized expense in one move. Red flag — large round-number transactions with a single counterparty near quarter-end.

Software — channel stuffing: a vendor ships far more product to distributors than they can sell, with a quiet right-of-return, booking it all as revenue to hit the quarter. Red flag — a Q4 sales spike followed by Q1 returns and bloated distributor inventory.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: when revenue rises but operating cash flow lags, follow the receivables. Genuine sales convert to cash; fictitious ones pile up as 'uncollected' balances.

t2.title: The five FSF scheme families & where they hide

body.h: Memorise these five — questions give a scenario and ask which family

table: Sales to fake or phantom customers; sham related-party sales.
Real revenue/expense in the wrong period (channel stuffing, premature recognition).
Omitting payables, warranty/litigation reserves; capitalizing operating costs.
Omitting related parties, contingencies, subsequent events, going-concern doubt.
Inflating inventory, receivables, or fixed assets; not writing down impaired assets.

body.key: 'December sales booked in November' = timing difference (real sale, wrong period). 'Failing to record warranty/litigation reserves' = concealed liabilities. 'Sales to a shell customer that doesn't exist' = fictitious revenue. The distinction is the whole game.

body.h: Frequency vs cost — the inverse law

body.p: Across all occupational fraud: asset misappropriation is most frequent but lowest median loss; financial statement fraud is least frequent but highest median loss; corruption sits in between. Expect at least one question on this ranking.

body.case: Retail/distribution — bill-and-hold: a manufacturer 'sells' goods but holds them in its own warehouse, booking revenue though the customer hasn't taken delivery or accepted risk. Tell — revenue recognized while inventory physically stays put and shipping docs are missing.

Manufacturing — cookie-jar reserves: in good years management over-accrues reserves, then quietly releases them in weak years to smooth earnings. Tell — reserve balances that move opposite to business conditions.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: improper disclosure fraud leaves no number wrong on the face of the statements — it hides in the notes. Always read related-party and subsequent-events footnotes against the transaction data.

t3.title: Cash-receipts schemes: skimming vs cash larceny

body.key: Skimming = theft of cash BEFORE it is recorded (off-book). No audit trail, because the sale/receipt was never entered. Cash larceny = theft AFTER it is recorded (on-book). A discrepancy appears between the records and the cash on hand (a drawer shortage).

body.p: So if an employee rings 'no sale' and pockets the cash → skimming (nothing recorded). If a cashier removes cash from a sale already recorded, creating a drawer shortage → cash larceny.

Lapping hides skimmed receivables: steal Customer A's payment, then post Customer B's later payment to A's account, then cover B with C — rolling the shortfall forward indefinitely. The classic tell is customer complaints that payments were misapplied or posted late. Independent reconciliation and customer confirmations break it.

Segregation of duties is the core control: whoever receives cash must not also record and reconcile it. Add surprise cash counts, independent bank reconciliations, and matching recorded sales to register tapes.

body.case: Casino — the cage & the rail: a cage cashier voids legitimate chip redemptions and keeps the cash before it's logged — off-book skimming. Casinos counter with the 'eye in the sky', mandatory dual control at the cage, and reconciling the drop box to logged transactions.

Restaurant/bar — the unrung drink: a bartender serves cash customers without ringing the sale, pocketing the money and keeping pour counts plausible. Tell — pour/usage variance: liquor consumed exceeds recorded sales.
Charity/collections — offering skimming: a volunteer counts cash donations alone and removes a cut before any record exists. Tell — donation income that doesn't track attendance or pledge data.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: skimming's defining weakness for the fraudster is that it caps how much they can take — once a sale is unrecorded, they can't easily inflate it. Larceny leaves a trail; skimming leaves a gap. Look for what's missing, not just what's wrong.

body.p: Disbursement schemes are on-book: the company's own funds leave through its accounting system on fraudulent documentation. These are the most common occupational frauds. Five families:

table: Shell-company invoices, personal purchases, inflated/duplicate invoices. Most common & costly.
Ghost employees, falsified hours/commissions, inflated pay rates.
Mischaracterized, overstated, fictitious, or duplicate claims.
Forged maker/endorsement, altered payee, authorized-maker abuse.
False refunds and false voids — a RECORDED transaction to justify removing cash.

body.key: Shell vs pass-through: a pure shell bills for goods/services never delivered; a pass-through (turnaround) actually buys real goods then resells them to the employer at an inflated markup. (So 'pass-through delivers nothing' is FALSE.)
Register disbursement ≠ skimming. A false refund is a recorded fraudulent transaction used to pull cash — the recorded entry is the giveaway. Skimming records nothing.

ul: Ghost employees: distribute paychecks in person and reconcile to active-HR records — no real person claims a ghost's check.
Check tampering is unique: the fraudster prepares or alters the instrument itself, not just the supporting document.
Expense mischaracterization: a genuine personal purchase reported as business (e.g., a personal laptop as 'client supplies').

body.case: Construction — over-billing & fake subs: a project manager sets up a shell 'subcontractor' and approves invoices for work never performed, buried in a large project's cost codes. Tell — a vendor with a PO box, no website, and invoices always just under the approval threshold.

Healthcare payroll — the ghost nurse: a supervisor keeps a terminated nurse 'active' and redirects the pay to a controlled account. Tell — an employee with no badge-ins, no benefits enrollment, and direct deposit to an account shared with another employee.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: billing schemes are the highest-frequency, highest-cost disbursement fraud — your VendorRecon territory. The fastest screens are duplicate-invoice tests, round-dollar invoices, vendors whose address matches an employee's, and invoices clustered just below approval limits.

t5.title: Inventory theft, corruption & conflicts of interest

body.p: Two routes: misuse (borrowing assets — low loss, hard to prove damages) and larceny (outright theft). Shrinkage — the unaccounted-for reduction in inventory — is the primary red flag; fraudsters keep it within 'normal' ranges to avoid scrutiny. Physical padding (stacking empty cartons during a count) fakes quantity on hand.

table: A thing of value to INFLUENCE a business decision (includes kickbacks).
A reward for a decision ALREADY made — no prior intent to influence.
The DEMAND side — an employee demands payment to decide in the payer's favour.
An undisclosed economic/personal interest in a transaction.

body.key: Bribery vs illegal gratuity turns entirely on timing/intent: bribery influences a future decision; an illegal gratuity rewards a past one. A kickback is a vendor returning part of an overbilling to the employee who steered the deal. A conflict of interest becomes fraud when the interest is undisclosed and divided loyalty harms the employer.

ul: Complementary (cover) bids — deliberately high bids to fake competition.
Bid suppression — agreeing not to bid.
Bid rotation — taking turns being the low bidder.
Market division — splitting territories/customers.

body.case: Casino — chip walking & comp abuse: a host with an undisclosed stake in a junket operator steers high-roller comps and rebates to that operator. Undisclosed interest + steering = conflict of interest layered with kickbacks.

Public works — the paving cartel: three contractors rotate who wins each municipal contract, submitting cover bids for the others. Tell — the same firms always bid, margins are suspiciously uniform, and the 'winner' rotates predictably.

Retail procurement — the slotting kickback: a category buyer awards premium shelf space to a supplier who funds the buyer's personal credit card. Tell — a mid-tier supplier consistently winning against stronger competitors.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: corruption is detected far more by tips and relationship analysis than by the books — the transaction often looks normal. Map employee-vendor connections, lifestyle changes, and exclusive-dealing patterns.

body.p: Bank fraud clusters around embezzlement, loan fraud, real-estate fraud, new-account fraud and wire fraud. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision sets global prudential standards (sound risk management) — distinct from FATF, which sets AML standards.

ul: Nominee / straw-borrower loan — loan in a front person's name for the real party's benefit (evades exposure limits, hides risk).
Loans to nonexistent borrowers and air loans (wholly fictitious property/borrower).
Double-pledged collateral; false applications (income/asset/occupancy misrepresentation).
Reciprocal loans between insiders to hide losses; construction draw fraud.

body.key: Appraisal (valuation) fraud — inflating a property's value to justify a larger mortgage — is your ValuGuard domain. Distinguish it from an air loan, which is on a property/borrower that doesn't exist at all.

body.p: The U.S. FCPA prohibits bribing foreign officials to obtain or retain business and requires accurate books & records plus internal accounting controls. The UK Bribery Act is broader (covers private bribery and 'failure to prevent').

body.case: Mortgage — the straw buyer ring: an organizer recruits people with clean credit to 'buy' inflated properties using a corrupt appraiser; loans fund, proceeds are split, and the straws walk away — the loans default. Tell — multiple loans, same appraiser, same closing agent, owner-occupancy claims that don't match utility records.

Trade finance — the phantom shipment: a borrower draws on a letter of credit using forged bills of lading for goods never shipped. Tell — shipping documents that don't reconcile to vessel/port records.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: insider involvement multiplies loss. The most damaging bank frauds pair an outsider's false application with an insider who waves it through — so test the approver, not just the applicant.

table: Dirty cash enters the system (deposits, structuring/smurfing, cash-intensive fronts).
Complex transfers obscure the source (shells, wire chains, cross-border movement).
'Clean' funds re-enter the economy as legitimate-looking assets (property, business, luxury).

body.key: Order: Placement → Layering → Integration. Structuring (smurfing) — breaking cash into sub-threshold deposits to dodge reporting — is a placement-stage red flag, and is an offence in itself even if the cash is from a legal source, because the intent is to defeat reporting. This is exactly the self-transfer / sub-threshold signal your StaffLens flags.

ul: FATF — issues the 40 Recommendations; the global AML/CFT standard-setter.
Egmont Group — links national Financial Intelligence Units; Wolfsberg principles; Basel guidance.
KYC/CDD, enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers, currency-transaction and suspicious-activity reporting.

body.p: Maps cleanly to India's PMLA: placement/layering/integration is the same language — but answer the exam in FATF/BSA framing.

body.case: Casino laundering: a launderer buys chips with dirty cash, gambles minimally, then cashes out asking for a casino cheque — 'clean' winnings. Counters: chip-purchase logging, cash-transaction reporting, and 'minimal-play cash-out' alerts.
Trade-based laundering: over- or under-invoicing exports moves value across borders disguised as trade. Tell — invoice prices wildly off market for the goods described.
Crypto layering: funds are split across wallets, run through mixers/tumblers, then consolidated and off-ramped. Tell — rapid many-hop transfers with no economic purpose.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: structuring is about intent to evade a threshold, not the amount. Many small, just-under-limit, round-number deposits across branches or days is the pattern — amount alone never proves it.

t8.title: Payment, identity, cyber, consumer & tax fraud

ul: Check kiting — exploiting the float (clearing delay) between two banks by passing checks against insufficient funds to fake a balance.
Payment-card fraud (skimming, card-not-present), electronic/P2P fraud, alternative currencies.
Synthetic identity theft — combine a real (stolen) ID number with a fabricated name/DOB to create a new identity. Distinct from account takeover (hijacking an existing account).
Business email compromise (BEC) — impersonate an executive/vendor by email to redirect a payment. Heavily emphasised in the 2026 blueprint.
Malware (ransomware, keyloggers), phishing/spear-phishing, the CIA triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability).

body.key: Ponzi pays 'returns' from new investors' money (no real returns). Pyramid derives income chiefly from recruitment, not product sales. Tax evasion is illegal and requires willful intent to defeat tax; tax avoidance is lawful minimization. The willfulness/legality line is the tested point.

body.case: Banking — the BEC wire: 'CEO' emails the AP clerk near closing on a Friday: urgent confidential acquisition, wire to this new account, don't call me. Tell — urgency + secrecy + a new beneficiary + a spoofed look-alike domain. Control: out-of-band callback verification on any change of payment details.

Insurance — staged accident ring: organized crews stage collisions and file inflated injury claims through complicit clinics and lawyers. Tell — same clinic, same attorney, soft-tissue injuries, identical treatment counts across unrelated 'victims'.

Elder fraud — the romance/advance-fee combo: a victim is groomed online, then asked for fees to release a fictitious fortune. Tell — escalating wire requests to overseas accounts, secrecy from family.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: BEC and kiting both exploit timing and trust, not broken controls. The defence is procedural — verification callbacks for payment changes, and monitoring inter-bank float and rapid in-out account activity.

body.h: Classify any cash scenario in one pass

body.key: Was it recorded? No → skimming. Recorded, then stolen → cash larceny. Paid out through the system on fake docs → fraudulent disbursement (then sub-classify: billing / payroll / expense / check / register).

ul: 'No-sale' rung, cash pocketed → skimming.
Customer A credited with B's payment → lapping.
Fake vendor, no goods → shell-company billing.
Real goods resold to employer at markup → pass-through.
Recorded false refund → register disbursement.
Empty cartons at the count → physical padding.
Reward after the award, no prior deal → illegal gratuity (not bribery).
Sub-threshold deposits → structuring (placement).

body.eye: Examiner's eye: most wrong answers are the adjacent scheme. Classify first from the facts, then confirm against the options — don't let a tempting near-miss pull you off.

body.p: A fraud examination is a methodology for resolving a specific allegation from inception to disposition — gathering evidence, taking statements, writing reports, testifying. It is not an audit: audits are recurring and general; examinations are specific and allegation-driven.

ol: Analyze available data.
Create a hypothesis (assume a worst-case scenario from the data).
Test the hypothesis against evidence.
Refine / amend as new facts emerge.

body.key: Two golden rules: conduct the exam general → specific, and interview least-culpable → most-culpable, so you reach the prime suspect last, armed with evidence.

body.p: Predication is the totality of circumstances that would lead a reasonable, professionally trained person to believe a fraud has occurred, is occurring, or will occur. No examination — and no admission-seeking interview or covert operation — begins without it. Mere suspicion isn't predication; 'fishing expeditions' violate the standard.

body.case: Manufacturing tip: an anonymous hotline call says a plant manager is steering scrap-metal sales to his cousin's yard below market. Combined with falling scrap revenue, that's predication — enough for a reasonable professional to open an exam, starting general (scrap process) before specific (the manager).

body.eye: Examiner's eye: write down your predication before you act. If you can't articulate why a reasonable professional would suspect fraud, you're not ready to start — and a defence lawyer will say so later.

t13.title: The law related to fraud: elements, burdens & systems

body.h: The four common-law elements of fraud

body.p: (1) a material false statement, (2) knowledge of its falsity, (3) victim reliance, and (4) resulting damages. Memorise these four — they recur across the section.

body.h: Burden of proof — the #1 Law trap

body.key: Lowest → highest: preponderance of the evidence ('more likely than not', civil) → clear and convincing → beyond a reasonable doubt (criminal). Criminal = state prosecutes, punishment; civil = private party, remedies/damages.

ul: Common law — judge-made precedent, adversarial (US/UK/India framework).
Civil law — codified statutes, inquisitorial.
Parallel proceedings — civil and criminal can run at once; manage self-incrimination and discovery conflicts.

body.case: Cross-border bank fraud: the same conduct triggers a criminal case (state, beyond a reasonable doubt) and a civil recovery suit by the bank (preponderance). The lower civil bar is why a defendant can be acquitted criminally yet still lose the civil case.

body.warn: This is your self-identified weak area. Drill the burden ladder and the four elements until automatic — they anchor most Law questions.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: 'material' and 'reliance' do real work. A false statement nobody relied on, or one too trivial to matter, often fails the legal test even when it feels dishonest.

t14b.title: Key statutes: SOX, RICO, False Claims Act, FCPA

body.h: The statutes the exam tests (in their framing)

ul: Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) — CEO/CFO certification of financials, stronger governance, whistleblower protection, criminal penalties for document destruction.
RICO — targets a pattern of racketeering activity; powerful criminal penalties and civil treble damages.
False Claims Act — fraud against the government; allows qui tam suits where a private 'relator' (whistleblower) sues on the government's behalf and shares any recovery.
Mail & wire fraud — broad federal hooks needing a scheme to defraud plus use of mail/wires.
FCPA — foreign bribery plus books-and-records and internal-control provisions.

body.key: Match the trigger word: 'pattern of racketeering' → RICO; 'whistleblower sues for the government and shares recovery' → qui tam / False Claims Act; 'CEO certifies the financials' → SOX; 'bribing a foreign official' → FCPA.

body.case: Healthcare — qui tam: a billing clerk discovers systematic Medicare upcoding and files a qui tam suit; the government intervenes and the relator shares the recovery. This whistleblower channel surfaces a large share of government-fraud cases.
Corporate — SOX document destruction: after a subpoena, staff shred engagement files. The shredding itself is a separate SOX offence, independent of the underlying fraud.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: these statutes are tested as recognition, not litigation. Lock the one-line trigger for each; you rarely need the sub-sections.

t14.title: Rights during investigations & basic evidence law

body.p: Constitutional criminal protections (4th/5th Amendment, Miranda) primarily restrain government action. A private employer is not required to give Miranda warnings before interviewing an employee — though employment law, contracts and policies still apply. (Garrity: public employees can't be forced to self-incriminate on threat of firing; Weingarten: union reps in investigatory interviews.)

body.key: Direct evidence proves a fact without inference (an eyewitness who saw the act). Circumstantial evidence requires an inference (fingerprints). Most fraud cases are built largely on circumstantial evidence — and that is fully valid and admissible. So 'fraud needs direct evidence' is FALSE.

ul: Relevant, material, competent evidence is admissible; hearsay generally excluded (with exceptions).
Attorney-client privilege and work-product doctrine protect materials — run exams under counsel to preserve them.
Chain of custody must be unbroken; a documented gap can render evidence inadmissible.

body.case: Procurement case: the only proof a manager rigged bids is circumstantial — his sister owns the winning vendor, bids were opened early, and prices track his emails. No eyewitness, yet the inference chain is strong enough to prove the case.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: juries are taught that circumstantial evidence is not 'weaker' than direct — a fingerprint can be more reliable than a nervous eyewitness. Build the inference chain tightly and document custody at every step.

ul: Obtain originals where possible; if copies, document why.
Maintain a chain-of-custody / evidence control log; handle minimally to preserve fingerprints, indented writing, ink/paper dating.
Never write on or annotate the original — it destroys evidentiary integrity.

ol: Preserve — image the drive with a write-blocker; never work on the original.
Maintain chain of custody for digital media just like physical evidence.
Analyze the forensic copy — recover deleted files, metadata, logs.
Document tools and hash values (MD5/SHA).

body.key: A matching hash value proves the forensic image is bit-for-bit identical to the original and unaltered — establishing integrity for court. Always analyze the image, never the original device. Cloud and mobile forensics are explicitly in the new blueprint.

body.case: IP theft — the departing engineer: before resigning, an engineer mass-copies designs to a USB drive. Examiners image his laptop (write-blocked), hash it, and recover USB-insertion artifacts and deleted file remnants — all from the copy, preserving the original for court.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the moment you boot a suspect's original device, you change it — last-access times, temp files, logs. That single mistake can get your best evidence thrown out. Image first, always.

body.h: The five question types — in order

ol: Introductory — build rapport, give a reason for the interview, get a commitment to cooperate (never accuse here).
Informational — open → closed → leading; gather the facts.
Closing — confirm facts, seek new info, maintain goodwill.
Assessment — establish credibility / detect deception (only when needed).
Admission-seeking — only when there is reasonable certainty of guilt.

body.key: Sequence is a guaranteed point: Introductory → Informational → Closing → Assessment → Admission-seeking. The last two are used only when warranted.

ul: Open — invites a narrative ('Tell me what happened').
Closed — specific, often yes/no.
Leading — contains its own answer ('You were in the vault that night, weren't you?'); used to confirm.
Avoid double-negative and overly complex questions.

body.p: Inhibitors of communication (ego threat, etiquette, trauma, forgetting) block disclosure; facilitators (recognition, sympathy, altruistic appeals) encourage it. The interviewer manages these deliberately. Conduct interviews privately, one subject at a time, documented.

body.case: Banking interview: investigating teller cash shortages, the examiner opens with rapport and a neutral reason ('reconciling some discrepancies'), uses open questions to let the teller narrate the day, and only narrows to leading questions once the timeline contradicts the logs.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the introductory phase isn't small talk — it sets whether the subject cooperates. Accuse too early and you lose the informational gold you haven't mined yet.

body.p: Only with reasonable certainty of guilt, conducted privately by an interviewer of suitable standing, after adequate predication. The goal is a voluntary, truthful confession.

ol: Direct accusation — stated with confidence, not as a question.
Observe reaction; repeat the accusation.
Interrupt denials — stop them before they harden (a firm denial is harder to retract).
Establish a rationalization (a morally acceptable theme) to lower resistance.
Diffuse alibis; display real evidence as needed.
Alternative question — two incriminating choices, one more face-saving ('Did you plan this, or did it just happen?').
Obtain a benchmark admission, then escalate to a full confession.
Obtain a signed written statement.

body.key: The alternative question is the pivotal technique. Interrupting denials before they entrench is equally tested.

body.warn: A signed statement is in the subject's own words, with dates, approximate amounts, intent, and an acknowledgment of voluntariness. Never promise leniency or non-prosecution — it can void the confession and exceeds your authority.

body.case: Retail — the sweethearting cashier: with CCTV and POS data already proving under-ringing for friends, the examiner accuses directly, interrupts the first denial, offers a face-saving theme ('Were you trying to help struggling friends, or just careless?'), and secures a written statement in the cashier's own words.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: no single verbal or non-verbal cue proves deception. Clusters matter — answering a question with a question, over-qualifying, selective memory, character testimony ('I'd never do that'). Treat cues as signals to probe, never as proof.

t18.title: Tracing assets, data analysis & sources of information

ul: Direct method — follow specific transactions through the records ('follow the money').
Indirect / circumstantial methods when records are incomplete:

table: Asset increases + living expenses − funds from known sources = likely illicit income. The headline indirect method.
Total deposits − transfers/known sources = understated income.

body.key: The net worth method is the most tested tracing technique: an unexplained rise in net worth plus living expenses, less funds from known legitimate sources, points to hidden/illicit income.

In naturally occurring amounts, leading digit 1 appears ~30.1% of the time, declining to ~4.6% for 9. Deviations flag possible manipulation. It applies to natural numbers (invoice/payment amounts), not assigned/sequential numbers (phone, account, ID, badge numbers).

body.case: Public-official case: a clerk earning a modest salary buys two flats and a luxury car in three years. The net worth method quantifies the gap between lifestyle and known income — the core of a disproportionate-assets case (and a familiar PMLA pattern).
AP fraud — Benford screen: running Benford's on a year of vendor payments shows a spike in amounts beginning '48' and '49' — clustering just under a ₹50,000 approval limit, exposing split invoices.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: Benford flags where to look, not guilt. A deviation is a lead; pair it with duplicate-payment and just-under-threshold tests before drawing conclusions.

ul: Criminal: charging → arraignment → trial → verdict → appeal (beyond a reasonable doubt).
Civil: complaint → discovery → trial → judgment/remedies (preponderance).
Parallel proceedings run both at once — manage self-incrimination and discovery carefully.

body.key: A lay witness testifies to facts personally observed; an expert witness (once qualified by the court) may give opinions within their expertise. On cross-examination, stay within expertise, concede what's genuinely true, don't advocate — and never express an opinion on the legal guilt or innocence of the accused. That's for the trier of fact.

ul: Accurate, clear, impartial, relevant, timely. Report facts, not conclusions of law or guilt.
Common mistakes: stating legal conclusions, opining on guilt, editorializing, omitting exculpatory evidence.
To protect privilege, conduct the investigation at the direction of counsel.
A covert operation needs adequate predication and a written memorandum of its basis and objectives before it begins.

body.case: Expert on the stand: asked point-blank 'So the defendant is guilty?', the examiner answers within bounds: 'My analysis shows ₹2.1 crore moved to accounts he controlled; whether that is criminal is for the court.' Findings, not a guilt verdict.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: a report that editorializes or buries exculpatory facts hands the defence its cross-examination. Write every line as if it will be read aloud to the jury — because it might be.

body.key: (1) burden-of-proof ladder, (2) four elements of fraud, (3) direct vs circumstantial, (4) chain of custody & hash integrity, (5) interview sequence, (6) admission-seeking steps & the alternative question, (7) net worth method & Benford scope, (8) never opine on guilt.

ul: 'More likely than not' → preponderance → civil.
Eyewitness saw it → direct; everything inferred → circumstantial.
Two incriminating choices offered → alternative question.
Unexplained wealth + living costs − known income → net worth method.
Leading-digit distribution on invoice amounts → Benford's Law.
Examiner asked if defendant is 'guilty' → improper; opine only within expertise.
Pattern of racketeering → RICO; whistleblower sues for the government → qui tam/FCA.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: if you remember nothing else from Section 2 — predication before you start, general-to-specific, least-to-most-culpable, preserve chain of custody, and never declare guilt.

ul: White-collar crime (Sutherland) — crime by a person of respectability and high social status in the course of their occupation.
Occupational fraud — using one's occupation for personal enrichment by misusing the employer's resources.
Organizational crime — offences committed by/for the organization itself.

body.h: The Fraud Triangle (Cressey) — the foundation of the whole exam

body.key: Pressure (a non-shareable financial problem) + Opportunity (a way to commit and conceal) + Rationalization (justifying it). Remove any leg and fraud is less likely. This is the single most-tested concept.

ul: Fraud Diamond — adds Capability (the person's position/skills/confidence to pull it off).
Fraud Scale (Albrecht) — pressure, opportunity, personal integrity.
Differential association (Sutherland) — fraud is learned behaviour, including its techniques and rationalizations, through association with others.

body.p: By frequency/cost: asset misappropriation (most frequent, lowest median loss) → corruption → financial statement fraud (least frequent, highest median loss). Tips are the #1 detection method. Longer schemes and higher perpetrator authority drive larger losses.

body.case: The trusted controller: a 20-year controller with gambling debts (pressure), sole control of payments and reconciliations (opportunity), telling himself he's 'just borrowing' (rationalization), and the system knowledge to hide it (capability). All four legs — the textbook long-running, high-authority, high-loss case.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: organizations can only really control opportunity — they can't fix an employee's debts or beliefs. That's why segregation of duties and monitoring matter so much: they attack the one leg you can remove.

t21b.title: Detection reality: tips, hotlines & the numbers

body.key: Tips are consistently the #1 detection method — well ahead of internal audit or external audit. Many tips come from employees, which is why a reporting hotline is one of the most effective anti-fraud controls: organizations with hotlines detect fraud faster and suffer lower losses.

body.p: This reframes prevention: the cheapest high-impact control is usually a well-run, well-publicised, anonymous reporting channel — not another layer of audit.

body.case: Hospitality chain: after launching an anonymous multilingual hotline with poster campaigns in back-of-house areas, a regional manager's kickback scheme surfaces within weeks via a line cook's tip — something three years of audits had missed.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: a hotline only works if staff trust it. Anonymity, non-retaliation, multiple channels (phone/web), and visible follow-through are what convert awareness into usable tips.

ul: Board (especially independent directors and the audit committee), management, internal & external auditors, regulators, shareholders.
The audit committee oversees financial reporting, internal control, and the external auditor — a key anti-fraud governance body.

body.key: Management — not the auditors — is primarily responsible for designing and maintaining internal controls and for preventing and detecting fraud. (So 'external auditors bear primary responsibility for controls' is FALSE.) Management also owns an effective compliance & ethics program and document-retention policies.

body.p: Tone at the top is the ethical climate leadership sets by example and messaging. A weak tone is the strongest cultural fraud-risk factor — controls underneath a corrupt leadership rarely hold.

body.case: The override case: a company has textbook controls on paper, but a dominant CEO routinely tells staff to 'just book it, I'll explain later.' The control design is irrelevant once leadership normalises override — exactly what governance and the audit committee exist to check.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: when assessing a control environment, watch what leaders tolerate, not what the policy manual says. Culture is revealed by the exceptions people are allowed to make.

ul: External — opinion on the financial statements; reasonable (not absolute) assurance they're free of material misstatement, including from fraud.
Internal — evaluate and improve governance, risk and control; report to the audit committee.
Government — compliance and performance audits.

body.key: An unqualified ('clean') opinion provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance. It is not a guarantee that no fraud exists — a classic distractor.

table: Foundation: integrity, ethical values, tone at the top, governance.
Identify and analyze risks to objectives.
Ongoing and separate evaluations of control effectiveness.

body.key: Five components; the control environment is the foundation. ('Fraud prosecution' is NOT a COSO component — a common trap.)

ul: Preventive (stop it — prior authorization, segregation of duties) vs Detective (find it — reconciliations, surprise audits, exception reports) vs Corrective.
Segregation of duties separates authorization, recording, and custody. Its absence is the most-cited control weakness.

body.case: Small-business reality: a 12-person firm can't fully segregate duties, so one bookkeeper authorizes, records, and reconciles. The compensating control is owner review of the bank statement before the bookkeeper sees it — a preventive/detective mix that attacks the opportunity leg.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: classify a control by when it acts. Prior authorization stops the payment (preventive); a reconciliation finds it afterward (detective). The exam loves this timing distinction.

t24.title: Fraud risk assessment, risk management, ethics & the CFE Code

body.key: Assess inherent risk first (before controls), then apply mitigating controls to reach residual risk. Prioritize by likelihood × significance (impact). An FRA is periodic and ongoing — not a one-time checkbox — and must respond to changes in the business.

ul: COSO/ACFE principles: governance, risk assessment, prevention & detection controls, investigation & corrective action, monitoring.
Third-party fraud risk — vendor/customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, contractual audit rights (your VendorRecon / DMA-scoring domain).
Most effective controls per ACFE: reporting hotlines, anti-fraud training, code of conduct, proactive data monitoring.

body.key: Two Code duties tested almost every sitting: (1) a member shall never express an opinion on the legal guilt or innocence of any person; (2) a member shall obtain evidence providing a reasonable basis for any opinion rendered. Also: maintain confidentiality, avoid undisclosed conflicts, and remember that legal does not always mean ethical.

body.case: Vendor onboarding: a procurement team scores new suppliers on red flags (shell-company markers, PO-box addresses, name-match to employees) before approval — an FRA applied to third-party risk, attacking opportunity before a single invoice is paid.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: an FRA that's filed and forgotten is worse than none — it creates false comfort. The value is in the refresh: new products, new vendors, new systems each open new fraud paths.

ul: Proactive elements: anti-fraud policy, code of conduct, ethics training, hotlines/whistleblower mechanisms, surprise audits, proactive data monitoring, a positive work environment.
Detection-by-tip dominance is why hotlines are emphasised — they speed detection and cut losses.

body.p: Distinguish morality, ethics, and legality — an act can be legal yet unethical. Apply professional skepticism and objectivity; avoid undisclosed conflicts of interest; hold to standards beyond the legal minimum.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: prevention isn't one control — it's a system where tone, training, hotlines, and monitoring reinforce each other. Any single control fails; the layered program is what deters.

body.p: Competitive intelligence is the lawful collection and analysis of public information about competitors. Espionage is obtaining that information through illegal or unethical means. The line is the method, not the information. Reading a rival's public filings, patents, job ads, and trade-show handouts is intelligence. Bribing their engineer, hacking their server, or lying about who you are to get it is espionage.

A trade secret must satisfy three tests: it has independent economic value from not being generally known, it is not readily ascertainable by proper means, and the owner took reasonable measures to keep it secret. That third element is the one companies fail — and the one exam questions hinge on. If the owner left it unprotected, it is not a trade secret at law, however valuable it was.

body.key: Trade secret = economic value from secrecy + not readily ascertainable + reasonable protective measures. Fail any one and the claim dies.

ul: Insiders — the largest single source. Departing employees taking client lists, source code, formulas.
Social engineering — pretexting a receptionist or help desk into disclosure.
Physical — dumpster diving, stolen laptops, unattended documents, shoulder surfing.
Electronic — network intrusion, malware, unsecured cloud storage, USB exfiltration.
Open sources — an aggregation of individually harmless public facts that together reveal a secret.
Surveillance — wiretapping, hidden recorders, telephoto photography of a plant.

body.p: Favourite targets of intelligence professionals are not the executives. They are the people with access but without security training: salespeople (who love to talk about the pipeline), engineers at conferences, secretaries and admin staff, and — above all — disgruntled or departing employees.

body.case: Case file — the resignation that wasn't sudden. A polymer firm's lead chemist resigns on a Friday and joins a rival on Monday. IT review shows that over the preceding eleven weeks he ran unusually large after-hours file transfers to a personal cloud account, and printed the master formula binder twice. Nothing was stolen physically. The forensic tell is the ramp-up before the resignation — data exfiltration is almost always visible in the 60–90 days preceding a departure, which is exactly why exit procedures that begin on the last day are useless. Note the firm's exposure: had it never required NDAs or marked the formula confidential, it would have no trade-secret claim at all, no matter how obvious the theft.

ul: Non-disclosure and non-compete agreements at hire, re-acknowledged at exit.
Classification and marking of confidential material — this is the 'reasonable measures' evidence.
Need-to-know access control; log and alert on bulk downloads.
Exit interviews that ask directly about retained materials and return of devices.
Electronic countersurveillance sweeps for bugs in sensitive meeting rooms.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: if the question asks whether an act was espionage or legitimate intelligence, ignore how valuable the information was and look only at how it was obtained. Deception, trespass, bribery, or interception = espionage. Public sources, however cleverly aggregated = intelligence, and lawful.

body.p: Identity theft is the wrongful obtaining and use of another person's identifying information for fraud. It is best understood in two stages: (1) acquisition of the data, and (2) use of it. Exam questions almost always test which stage a described act belongs to, and which type of scheme it became.

body.h: Types of identity theft — memorise the distinctions

ul: Financial identity theft — using the identity to obtain credit, goods, or services. The most common.
Criminal identity theft — giving the victim's name to police on arrest. The victim discovers it via a warrant or a failed background check.
Identity cloning — the thief lives as the victim, assuming the identity wholesale rather than monetising it once.
Medical identity theft — using the identity to obtain treatment or drugs. Uniquely dangerous because it corrupts the victim's medical record.
Synthetic identity theft — a fabricated identity built from real fragments (often a real but unused SSN combined with a false name and DOB). No single victim complains, so it survives far longer.
Child identity theft — a minor's clean, unmonitored identity; typically undiscovered for years, until the child first applies for credit.

body.key: Synthetic identity theft is the highest-growth and hardest-to-detect variety precisely because there is no natural victim to raise the alarm. Traditional identity theft has a person who notices; synthetic has none.

ul: Phishing (mass email), spear phishing (targeted at a named individual), vishing (voice), smishing (SMS).
Pretexting — a fabricated scenario to extract data ('I'm from your bank's fraud team').
Skimming — a card-reading device on an ATM or POS terminal (distinguish this from cash-receipts skimming — the exam will try this trap).
Dumpster diving, mail theft, shoulder surfing.
Data breaches and insider theft of customer databases.
Pharming — DNS redirection to a spoofed site even though the victim typed the correct address.

body.case: Case file — the mortgage that belonged to nobody. A lender's fraud unit finds a borrower with a thin but clean file: valid SSN, three years of credit history, a modest card paid perfectly, no derogatory marks — and no employment that can be verified beyond a single pay stub. The SSN traces to a child. This is a synthetic identity in the 'nurturing' phase: the fraudster built credit patiently for years, then applied for a large loan intending to bust out — max every line and vanish. The red flag was never a bad record; it was an implausibly thin but perfect one, with no verifiable physical footprint.

ul: Place a fraud alert / freeze with the credit bureaus.
Report to the relevant national authority and obtain a report — this is what creditors require.
File a police report.
Notify affected creditors in writing; close and reissue compromised accounts.
Retain copies of every communication.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: 'skimming' means two entirely different things in this manual. In cash receipts it is off-book theft before recording. In identity theft it is a card-data capture device. Read the surrounding facts, not the word.

body.p: This chapter is your professional home ground, but the exam frames it in US/international terms. Learn the ACFE's names for schemes you already investigate daily.

ul: False accounting entries — debiting a customer account, crediting the insider's.
Unauthorised withdrawals and unauthorised disbursement of funds to outsiders.
Paying personal expenses from bank funds; theft of physical property.
Moving money to shell/suspense accounts, then out.
Loans to non-existent borrowers — fictitious loan proceeds taken by the insider.
Sham loans with kickbacks; linked financing (loan proceeds cycle back to buy the lender's own stock or property at inflated value).
Double-pledging collateral — the same asset secures multiple loans at different lenders.
Reciprocal loan arrangements — two insiders at different banks lend to each other's interests to conceal.
Daisy chain — a group passes an asset among themselves at escalating prices to inflate value before pledging.
Construction loan fraud — draws requested for work not performed; overstated percentage of completion.
Credit-data blocking / false loan applications — falsified income, employment, or asset documentation.

body.key: Linked financing: large deposits are offered to a bank on condition that it makes a loan to a designated party. The deposit is the bait; the bad loan is the payoff.

ul: Appraisal fraud — inflated valuation to support an oversized loan. (Your ValuGuard territory.)
Air loans — no property, no borrower, no collateral. Pure fabrication.
Property flipping — buy, fraudulently appraise high, resell quickly to a straw buyer.
Straw buyer — a person who lends their name and credit for a fee; the true purchaser stays hidden.
Equity skimming — take title, collect rents, never service the mortgage, let it foreclose.
Fraudulent foreclosure rescue — a distressed owner is induced to sign over title.
New account fraud — an account opened with a false or stolen identity, used to deposit stolen or counterfeit instruments.
Advance-fee fraud — a fee demanded for a loan or windfall that never arrives.
Letter-of-credit fraud — forged or fictitious LCs, or presentation of falsified shipping documents.
Wire transfer fraud — dishonest bank employee, false authorisation, or intercepted instructions.
Account takeover — an existing legitimate account seized via credential theft.
Inside/outside frauds — an employee colluding with an outsider; the classic and hardest case.

body.case: Case file — the daisy chain. Four related parties buy a warehouse for 400,000, then sell it among themselves in three quick arm's-length-looking transactions at 700,000, 1.1m, and 1.6m. The last owner pledges it to a bank as collateral for a 1.3m loan, using the most recent sale as the comparable. The bank's appraiser saw a genuine recent sale at 1.6m and had no reason to doubt it. The tell was never the appraisal — it was the transaction velocity between related parties with no improvement to the asset. Value cannot quadruple in six months with no capital works. Always trace the chain of title, not just the last price.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: distinguish who is defrauding whom. Embezzlement = insider steals from the bank. Loan fraud = borrower (or insider colluding) obtains funds the bank would not otherwise lend. New-account and advance-fee = outsiders using the bank as an instrument. The scheme name follows the direction of the theft.

body.p: A security is broader than 'a share'. Under the classic Howey test, an investment contract exists where there is (1) an investment of money, (2) in a common enterprise, (3) with an expectation of profits, (4) derived predominantly from the efforts of others. That last element is decisive: if the investor's own labour drives the return, it is not a security.

body.key: Howey: money + common enterprise + expectation of profit + profits from the efforts of OTHERS. The orange grove sold with a management contract was a security; the grove sold alone was not.

ul: Ponzi scheme — earlier investors paid from later investors' principal. There is no real underlying investment. It collapses when redemptions exceed new money.
Pyramid scheme — returns come from recruiting. Distinguish from a lawful MLM: a pyramid's compensation is driven by recruitment, not by retail sale of a real product to end users.
Pump and dump — accumulate a thinly traded stock, hype it (spam, boiler room, false press), sell into the retail buying, price collapses.
Insider trading — trading on material, non-public information in breach of a duty. Both elements matter: information that is non-public but immaterial, or material but public, is not enough.
Churning — a broker over-trades a client's account to generate commissions. Requires control over the account plus excessive trading given the client's objectives.
Front running — the broker trades ahead of a large client order it knows is coming.
Boiler room — high-pressure telephone sales of dubious or non-existent securities.
Unsuitable recommendations — a product mismatched to the client's risk profile, age, or objectives.

body.case: Case file — Ponzi or pyramid? A promoter sells 'agricultural bonds' promising 3% monthly. Investors receive their 3% for fourteen months. No farm exists; each payment comes from new subscriptions. This is a Ponzi — the investor is passive and paid from later principal. Change one fact: investors are told they must each enrol two more investors to qualify for payouts. Now it is a pyramid — return depends on recruitment by the investor. The money mechanics look identical; the classification turns on where the return is said to come from.

ul: Consistent, smooth returns regardless of market conditions — real markets are not smooth.
Returns well above market with claimed low risk.
Secrecy about strategy, or a strategy 'too complex to explain'.
Difficulty withdrawing; pressure to reinvest.
Unregistered products, unlicensed sellers, self-custody of assets, no independent auditor.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: Ponzi = passive investors paid from later investors' principal. Pyramid = investors paid for recruiting. Both are unsustainable, but the exam wants the mechanism, not the outcome.

ul: Forged maker — the signature of the drawer is forged. The cheque is stolen blank and signed.
Forged endorsement — a genuine cheque, made out to a real payee, is stolen and the payee's endorsement is forged.
Altered cheque — a genuine, properly signed cheque whose payee or amount has been changed.
Counterfeit cheque — the instrument itself is fabricated.
Cheque kiting — exploiting the float between two or more accounts at different banks, writing cheques against uncollected funds to create fictitious balances.
Cheque tampering — an employee converting the employer's own cheques (this is the fraudulent-disbursement scheme from your earlier study — note it appears in both chapters).

body.key: Forged maker = the drawer's signature is fake. Forged endorsement = the payee's signature is fake, and the cheque itself was genuine. This single distinction is tested almost every sitting.

body.h: Cheque kiting — how to spot it

ul: Frequent deposits and withdrawals with nearly identical amounts.
A pattern of deposits from, and withdrawals to, the same set of accounts at other banks.
Heavy activity in a low-balance account; frequent enquiries about the available balance.
A rising volume of deposited items drawn on the account holder's own other accounts.
The classic mathematical tell: average daily float greatly exceeds average ledger balance.
Counterfeit / cloned cards from skimmed track data.
Card-not-present (CNP) — online or phone use of stolen numbers. Now the dominant form.
Lost / stolen card use; never-received issue (NRI) — intercepted in the mail.
Account takeover — the fraudster changes the address, then reports the card lost and has a replacement sent.
Bust-out — build a good payment record, then max all lines and disappear.
Merchant / factoring fraud — a complicit merchant processes fraudulent charges, or launders another merchant's transactions through its own account.
Carding — testing stolen numbers with small transactions before a large one.
Business email compromise (BEC) — spoofed or hijacked email directing a payment to a fraudster's account. Test: was the account detail change verified out-of-band?
P2P payment fraud — irrevocable transfers induced by deception; no chargeback rights.

Cryptocurrency — pseudonymous, irreversible, and cross-border, which is why it is a laundering and ransom vector. Note it is pseudonymous, not anonymous: the blockchain is a permanent public ledger and is traceable at the on/off ramps.

body.case: Case file — the kite that flew for nine months. A small distributor holds accounts at Bank A and Bank B. Each Monday it deposits a 90,000 cheque drawn on B into A, and on Tuesday a 95,000 cheque drawn on A into B — each covering the other, each slightly larger. Neither account ever holds real money; the balances are pure float. It collapsed only when Bank A shortened its clearing window by one day. The detection signal was available for months: deposits and withdrawals in matched pairs, between the same two accounts, with amounts escalating. No single transaction looked wrong.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: kiting creates value out of float — the fraud is the timing gap, not the instrument. If the fact pattern involves two banks and matched round-trip cheques, it is kiting, whatever else it is dressed as.

body.p: Classify insurance fraud by who commits it. The exam's answer options are usually built along this axis: the policyholder/claimant, the agent/broker, the insurer itself, or an internal employee.

ul: Premium diversion — the agent collects premium and never remits it to the insurer. The most common agent fraud; the insured discovers it only on making a claim and finding no policy.
Fictitious payees / phantom policies — policies written on non-existent people to earn commission.
Churning — inducing replacement of policies to generate fresh commissions, to the client's detriment.
Sliding — adding coverage the client did not ask for and did not knowingly agree to.
Twisting — misrepresenting facts to persuade a client to switch insurers.
Fraudulent underwriting — misstating risk facts on the application to secure a lower premium.

body.key: Churning = replacing a policy within the same insurer for commission. Twisting = inducing a switch to another insurer by misrepresentation. Sliding = charging for coverage the client never agreed to.

body.h: Claimant fraud by line of business

ul: Vehicle — staged accidents (deliberate collisions, often with a 'swoop and squat' set-up), owner give-ups (the owner arranges the theft or destruction of their own vehicle), inflated repair estimates, phantom passengers claiming injury.
Property — arson for profit (look for over-insurance, financial distress, removal of valuables before the fire), inflated inventories of destroyed contents, claims for items never owned.
Life — false death claims (faked death, or 'pseudocide'), murder for proceeds, fraudulent applications concealing terminal illness, forged beneficiary changes.
Liability — slip-and-fall staging, exaggerated soft-tissue injury (hard to disprove, hence popular).
Workers' compensation — this is the big one for the exam (see below).

body.h: Workers' compensation fraud — know these four

ul: Premium fraud (by the employer) — understating payroll, misclassifying employees into lower-risk categories, or misrepresenting the claims history to reduce premium.
Claimant fraud — a non-existent injury, an injury sustained off the job reported as work-related, or malingering long after recovery.
Organised fraud — a ring of a lawyer, a doctor (a 'capper' or 'runner' recruits claimants), and the claimant, generating fabricated medical bills.
Agent fraud — collecting premium for a policy never placed.

body.case: Case file — the fire that told on itself. A struggling furniture retailer suffers a total-loss fire on a Sunday night. Red flags stack: the policy limit was doubled eleven weeks earlier; the business had three months of unpaid suppliers; the fire began in two separate, unconnected points (a physical impossibility for an accident); and the CCTV recorder — which the owner insisted was 'always on' — was removed the previous Friday. Note the pattern: motive (distress) + opportunity (recent over-insurance) + physical evidence inconsistent with accident. Arson-for-profit cases are almost always proven on the financial record, not the fire scene.

ul: Claim filed shortly after policy inception or after a limit increase.
Claimant is over-eager to settle, or unusually familiar with claims terminology and procedure.
No police or fire report where one would be expected; pressure against involving authorities.
Injuries that are subjective and unverifiable; the same doctor/lawyer recurring across unrelated claims.
Post-dated or backdated documents; receipts that are too neat, sequential, or from a single source.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: 'the claim came shortly after a coverage increase' and 'the same medical provider appears on unrelated claims' are the two facts the ACFE plants most often. When you see either, the answer is an organised or premeditated scheme, not opportunism.

body.p: Health care fraud is largely a billing fraud. The service is the cover; the claim form is the instrument. Classify by actor: provider, medical staff, institution, patient, insurer, or employee/agent.

body.h: Provider billing schemes — learn these names exactly

ul: Upcoding — billing for a more expensive procedure or a higher level of service than was actually performed. The single most tested term in this chapter.
Unbundling (fragmentation) — splitting one bundled procedure into its component parts and billing each separately, to collect more than the bundled rate.
Phantom billing / billing for services not rendered — the service never happened at all.
Duplicate billing — the same service billed twice, or to two payers.
Overutilisation — medically unnecessary services, tests, or admissions performed to generate billings.
Ping-ponging — referring a patient among several practitioners in the same clinic, each billing a consultation.
Gang visits / family ganging — billing for services to multiple family members when only one was seen, or a nursing-home 'round' billed as individual visits.
Steering — pushing patients toward an entity in which the provider has an undisclosed interest (self-referral).
DRG creep — an institution systematically coding admissions into higher-reimbursing diagnosis groups.

body.key: Upcoding = charging for a bigger service than performed. Unbundling = charging separately for parts of one service. Both inflate the claim, but the mechanism differs — and the exam will offer both as options.

body.p: Kickbacks in health care are structurally identical to the corruption schemes you already know, but the payer is a reimbursement system rather than a purchaser. Watch for: payments for patient referrals; 'consulting' or 'medical director' fees far above fair market value; free or below-cost rent or equipment; sham research grants; and waiver of patient co-payments (which removes the patient's only price signal and is itself an inducement).

ul: Patient — doctor shopping for prescriptions, lending an insurance card, staging or exaggerating injury, forging prescriptions.
Institution — cost-report fraud (padding allowable costs), false certifications of medical necessity, fraud in special-care facilities (billing for care not given to residents who cannot complain).
Insurer — selling non-existent or unlicensed health plans, wrongful and systematic claim denial, failing to remit premiums.
Employee claims fraud — false claims filed by employees under a group plan.
Electronic claims fraud — automated submission of fraudulent claims at volume; a single compromised provider ID can generate thousands.

body.case: Case file — fifteen-minute days. An audit of a physician's claims shows he billed a mean of 14.2 hours of face-to-face patient contact per working day, including a Tuesday on which the claim data implies 26 hours. No individual claim was implausible; each described an ordinary consultation at an ordinary rate. The fraud was invisible at the transaction level and obvious in the aggregate. This is why health care fraud is a data-analytics discipline: build the provider's implied working day, compare each provider against peer norms for the same specialty, and the outliers surface themselves. Chasing individual claim forms will never find it.

ul: Provider billings far exceeding peer norms for the specialty; impossible service volumes per day.
A high proportion of claims at the highest-value code (upcoding tells).
Routine waiver of co-pays; patients who cannot recall receiving the billed service.
Diagnosis inconsistent with the patient's demographics or history.
Corporate compliance programme absent, or existing only on paper.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the giveaway phrase for upcoding is 'billed at a higher level than the service provided'. The giveaway for unbundling is 'billed separately for components normally reimbursed as one'. Do not let them blur.

body.p: This chapter is a taxonomy. The ACFE tests whether you can put a described scam in the right named box. Learn the names.

ul: Advance-fee scheme — a payment demanded up front for a loan, prize, inheritance, or windfall that never materialises. The umbrella under which many others sit.
Nigerian / 419 letter — the classic advance-fee variant: help move a fortune, pay the 'transfer fee'.
Pyramid & Ponzi — as under securities fraud; when sold to retail consumers they appear here too.
Chain letter — a pyramid stripped of any product.
Multi-level marketing (MLM) — lawful where compensation flows from genuine retail sales to end users; becomes an unlawful pyramid where it flows from recruitment and inventory loading.
Telemarketing fraud — high-pressure phone sales; reloading is the key term: returning to a known prior victim for a second bite, often posing as a recovery agent.
Recovery-room / reload scheme — offering, for a fee, to recover the money the victim lost in an earlier scam. Victim lists are a traded commodity.
Travel & vacation scams — free-holiday certificates with escalating hidden fees; phantom timeshares.
Home-improvement / repair fraud — the itinerant contractor, the unnecessary repair, the vanishing deposit.
Debt consolidation & credit-repair fraud — a fee for services that are free, or for illegal 'file segregation' (creating a new credit identity).
Work-at-home / employment schemes — a fee for materials, kits, or 'certification'; the reshipping and money-mule variants make the victim an unwitting launderer.
Romance / relational fraud — a cultivated relationship, then a crisis requiring money. Now among the highest-loss consumer frauds.
Charity fraud — solicitation for a non-existent or misrepresented cause, spiking after disasters.

body.key: Reloading is the term to remember: the fraudster returns to an already-defrauded victim. Victims of one scam are the most valuable prospects for the next — which is why 'sucker lists' are bought and sold.

ul: Artificial urgency and a closing deadline.
Demand for an irrevocable payment method — wire, gift card, crypto, cash courier.
An appeal to secrecy: 'don't tell your bank/family, they'll try to stop you'.
Reciprocity: a small gift, sample, or 'prize' that creates obligation.
Social proof and manufactured authority — fake reviews, forged credentials, spoofed caller ID.

body.p: The ACFE's data does not support the folk belief that the elderly are universally the most victimised. The elderly suffer higher losses per incident (they hold more assets and are targeted for it), but younger, more online-active consumers report fraud more frequently. If an option says 'the elderly are the most frequently victimised group', treat it with suspicion — frequency and severity are different measures.

body.case: Case file — the second theft. A retiree loses 40,000 to a fake investment. Four months later she is telephoned by a 'fraud recovery bureau' that knows the exact amount she lost and the name of the fake firm — proof, she thinks, of legitimacy. They require a 3,000 'court filing fee'. She pays. It is the same organisation, working its own victim list. The knowledge of her loss was never evidence of authenticity; it was evidence of identity. Anyone contacting a victim already knowing the details of the original fraud should be presumed connected to it.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: for pyramid-vs-MLM questions, ask a single question — does the money come from selling a real product to real end users, or from recruiting? Inventory loading (recruits forced to buy stock they cannot sell) is the tell for an unlawful pyramid.

body.p: Bankruptcy fraud is fraud using the insolvency process — either to hide assets from creditors, or to loot a business behind the shield of the proceeding.

body.h: Key parties — learn who does what

ul: Debtor — the person or entity that owes.
Creditor — secured or unsecured; priority determines who gets paid first.
Trustee — administers the estate, collects and liquidates assets, and investigates the debtor's affairs. The trustee is the fraud examiner's natural ally.
Examiner — appointed where fraud or mismanagement is suspected; investigates but does not administer.
Debtor in possession — in a reorganisation, the debtor retains control of the business, with fiduciary duties to creditors.
Liquidation (US: Chapter 7) — assets sold, proceeds distributed, debts discharged.
Reorganisation (US: Chapter 11) — the business continues and restructures its debts.
Adjustment of debts (US: Chapter 13) — an individual with regular income repays over a plan period.
Concealment of assets — by far the most common bankruptcy fraud. Assets transferred to relatives or shells, or simply omitted from the schedules.

Bust-out — the signature scheme: a business builds credit, orders large inventory on credit, sells it fast (often below cost, for cash), diverts the proceeds, then files for bankruptcy leaving suppliers unpaid. Planned insolvency from the outset.
Petition mills — a 'service' purporting to help distressed tenants or debtors, which instead files bankruptcy on their behalf and strips fees.
Multiple filings — the same debtor files in several jurisdictions, or under variant identities, to delay creditors.
Credit-card bust-out — max the lines, then file.
Fraudulent transfers / preferences — moving assets out, or paying favoured creditors, in the period before filing.
Embezzlement by the trustee or fiduciary — rare but severely punished.
False statements / perjury in the schedules — the charge that most bankruptcy fraud actually gets prosecuted under.

body.key: Bust-out: build credit → load up on inventory bought on credit → liquidate it for cash → divert the cash → file for bankruptcy. If a fact pattern shows a sudden surge of credit purchases followed shortly by insolvency, it is a bust-out.

ul: A sharp, unexplained increase in credit purchases shortly before filing.
Inventory sold well below cost, or for cash, or to related parties.
Recent transfers of property to family members or newly formed entities.
Books and records 'lost', destroyed, or unavailable.
A change of business name, location, or management shortly before filing.
Lifestyle of the principals unaffected by the claimed insolvency.

body.case: Case file — the wholesaler who ordered too well. An electronics distributor with a five-year record of steady, modest ordering suddenly triples its purchases across eleven suppliers within a single quarter, all on 60-day terms. Goods move out at 60% of cost through a cash-only outlet. Two weeks after the last delivery, it files. Directors' bank accounts show corresponding deposits. Every element of the bust-out is present: the credit history was the asset being spent. The distributor spent five years building the very trust it was about to liquidate — which is why the surge, not the failure, is the detectable moment.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: concealment of assets is the most common bankruptcy fraud; bust-out is the most tested. Do not confuse the two — concealment hides what exists, bust-out manufactures the insolvency.

body.p: The whole chapter turns on one distinction.

body.key: Tax avoidance = lawfully arranging affairs to minimise tax. Tax evasion = unlawfully concealing or misrepresenting to escape tax. The difference is legality and intent, not the size of the saving.

body.p: To prove evasion you generally need: (1) an additional tax due and owing, (2) an affirmative act of evasion — not mere omission — and (3) wilfulness, a voluntary and intentional violation of a known legal duty. Negligence, a genuine mistake, or a good-faith misunderstanding of a complex provision is not evasion, because wilfulness fails.

ul: Understating income — omitting cash receipts, skimming before the books, unreported side businesses.
Overstating deductions — fictitious expenses, personal costs claimed as business, inflated charitable valuations.
Fictitious dependants / false credits.
Improper allocation of income — shifting income to a lower-taxed entity, jurisdiction, or family member without substance.
Offshore concealment — undisclosed foreign accounts, nominee and shell structures.
False books, two sets of records, destruction of records.
Transfer pricing abuse — mispricing intra-group transactions to move profit to low-tax jurisdictions.
Payroll tax fraud — withholding employee tax and never remitting it; treating employees as contractors.
Refund fraud / stolen-identity refund fraud — filing a return in the victim's name to capture their refund. The victim discovers it when their genuine return is rejected as a duplicate.
Preparer fraud — a preparer inflates deductions (often without the client's knowledge), or diverts the refund to their own account.
Impersonation scams — callers posing as the tax authority demanding immediate payment by irrevocable means. A real revenue authority does not demand gift cards.

body.p: Because direct evidence of unreported income is rare, examiners rely on indirect methods — the same ones in the Tracing Assets chapter: the net worth method (assets − liabilities, adjusted for known income and living expenses; an unexplained increase implies unreported income), the expenditures method, and the bank deposits method. Expect at least one question linking tax evasion to the net worth method.

body.case: Case file — a lifestyle that didn't add up. A restaurateur declares annual income of 30,000. Over four years his net worth rises by 480,000 — two properties, no mortgage, and school fees of 60,000 a year. He has no inheritance, no loans, no gifts. The net worth method imputes the unreported income: the increase in wealth plus living expenses, less known reported sources, is income he must explain. He need not confess; the arithmetic is the evidence. Note the affirmative act required for evasion — here, the maintenance of a second set of till records made it wilful, not merely careless.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: if a fact pattern stresses that the taxpayer used an aggressive but disclosed structure, the answer is avoidance. If it stresses concealment, false documents, or a second set of books, the answer is evasion. Look for the affirmative act.

body.p: For the exam, cyberfraud is a vocabulary chapter. You do not need to be a technologist; you need to attach the right name to the right described behaviour.

body.h: Malware — the taxonomy that gets tested

ul: Virus — attaches to a host file and requires user action to execute and spread.
Worm — self-replicating and self-propagating; needs no host file and no user action. This virus/worm distinction is a near-certain question.
Trojan horse — masquerades as legitimate software; does not self-replicate.
Ransomware — encrypts data and demands payment for the key.
Spyware / keylogger — covertly records activity or keystrokes.
Rootkit — conceals the intruder's presence at a deep system level.
Logic bomb — dormant code that triggers on a condition (a date, or the deletion of the author's payroll record — the classic disgruntled-insider weapon).
Botnet — a network of compromised machines under a single controller; the engine behind DDoS and spam.
Scareware — false warnings inducing the purchase of bogus 'security' software.

body.key: Virus needs a host and a user. A worm needs neither. If the fact pattern says it spread across the network without anyone opening anything, it is a worm.

ul: Social engineering — still the most effective intrusion vector. Technology is not the weak point; people are.
Phishing / spear phishing / whaling — mass, targeted, and executive-targeted respectively.
SQL injection — malicious input exploiting an unsanitised database query.
Cross-site scripting (XSS); buffer overflow.
Man-in-the-middle — interception and possible alteration of communications in transit.
DoS / DDoS — exhausting capacity to deny service; note this is disruption, not data theft.
Brute force and credential stuffing (reusing breached passwords elsewhere).
Zero-day — exploiting a vulnerability before a patch exists.
Pharming — DNS poisoning that redirects a correctly typed address to a spoofed site.
Spoofing — falsifying the origin of an email, IP, or caller ID.
Salami technique — slicing tiny amounts (rounding fractions) from many accounts; individually invisible, collectively large.

body.p: The insider is the hardest cyber threat because access is legitimate. Watch for: privilege creep (access accumulating across role changes and never revoked), shared or generic administrator accounts (which destroy attribution), after-hours access without business reason, and access by employees under notice of termination.

body.case: Case file — the logic bomb. A systems administrator, aware he is about to be made redundant, plants code that checks the payroll database nightly for his own employee ID. If the ID is absent, the code begins deleting production servers. He is terminated on a Friday; the servers fail on the following Wednesday. Note the anti-fraud control that would have stopped it and was absent: immediate revocation of privileged access at termination, and code review with segregation of duties. The single most dangerous person in an organisation is a privileged technical employee with a grievance and continuing access.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: DoS/DDoS is about availability, not confidentiality — no data is stolen. If an option describes 'stealing data by overwhelming a server with traffic', it is wrong on the mechanism.

body.p: You already know the corruption chapter. This one puts it inside a contracting process. The exam wants you to place the scheme at the correct phase of that process.

ul: Presolicitation — the need is identified and specifications are written. Schemes here: need recognition fraud (an unnecessary purchase is manufactured), and bid tailoring / specification fraud (specs written so that only one favoured vendor can qualify).
Solicitation — the request goes out and bids are invited. Schemes here: bid manipulation, bid rigging, leaking of bid data.
Bid evaluation & award — Schemes here: bid rigging via a corrupt evaluator, manipulation of scoring, unjustified sole-source award.
Post-award / performance — Schemes here: product substitution, defective pricing, cost mischarging, change-order abuse.

body.key: Phase matters. Bid tailoring happens before the tender is issued (in the specifications). Bid rigging happens during solicitation and evaluation. The exam distinguishes them by when.

body.h: Collusion among bidders — the four named forms

ul: Complementary bidding (cover / courtesy bidding) — competitors submit deliberately high or unacceptable bids to create the appearance of competition. The most common form.
Bid rotation — the conspirators take turns being the low bidder, on a schedule.
Bid suppression — competitors agree to withdraw, or not to bid at all.
Market division — competitors carve up territories or customers and do not bid against each other.
Product substitution — delivering goods of lower quality or non-conforming specification while billing for the specified item.
Defective pricing — submitting cost or pricing data that is not current, accurate, or complete, to inflate a negotiated price.
Cost mischarging — charging costs to the wrong contract (typically a cost-plus contract) or claiming unallowable costs.
Change-order abuse — a low bid wins, then the price is recovered through a stream of inflated change orders. Detect via: the winner bid unusually low, then generated abnormally many changes.
Progress-payment fraud — billing for a stage of completion not reached.
Grant fraud — funds diverted from the stated purpose; false progress reports.
Benefit / entitlement fraud — payments claimed for ineligible or non-existent recipients (ghost beneficiaries).
Payroll & ghost employees in the public body itself.
Bribery of officials; bid-data leakage by an insider.
Conflict of interest — an official with an undisclosed interest in a bidder. Note: a conflict of interest need not involve any payment — the undisclosed interest is itself the violation.
Revolving-door abuse — an official steering a contract to a future employer.

body.case: Case file — the cover bids. Over three years a municipality awards eleven road contracts. In every tender the same four firms bid; the winner rotates in a near-perfect cycle; and the losing bids are consistently 18–22% above the winner — too uniform to be the product of independent estimating. One losing bid contains a spreadsheet with the winner's letterhead in the document metadata. This is complementary bidding plus bid rotation.
