c3_s3.scenario: A lender's internal audit examines a loan officer with unusually high origination volume and near-zero early-payment defaults — until a cluster of his loans defaulted simultaneously after their first payment. Review shows several borrowers cannot be located, share mailing addresses with one another, and list employers whose telephone numbers all route to the same voicemail. Loan proceeds in several files were disbursed to a common third-party account. The officer had sole control of origination, verification, and disbursement for these files.
o: Ordinary credit losses in a downturn
A borrower-side conspiracy the lender could not have prevented
Insider loan fraud using fictitious or straw borrowers, enabled by absence of segregation of duties
c3_s3.e: Unlocatable borrowers, shared addresses and a single employer voicemail, common disbursement account, and one officer controlling the whole file point to insider loan fraud with fictitious/straw borrowers. The simultaneous first-payment defaults are the give-away that the borrowers were never real. The absence of segregation of duties enabled it — so it was preventable (contra A). Not ordinary losses (A); not takeover of existing accounts (B).

c3_s4.t: Referring to the same scenario, which control failure was the MOST significant enabler?
o: One individual controlling origination, verification, and disbursement without independent checks
c3_s4.e: Concentration of origination, verification, and disbursement in one person removed every independent check that would have caught fictitious borrowers — the core segregation-of-duties failure. Interest-rate risk (B) and marketing (D) are unrelated; a weak reserve (A) affects loss absorption, not prevention.

c3_j3.t: Which scenario is the STRONGEST indicator of double-pledged collateral?
o: A borrower's collateral has fallen in value
A borrower has loans at two different lenders
The same specific asset appears as security in the loan files of two different lenders, neither aware of the other
A borrower repaid one loan early
c3_j3.e: Double-pledging is the same asset secured to multiple lenders unaware of one another. Merely holding loans at two lenders (B) is ordinary. Falling collateral value (A) and early repayment (D) are unrelated. The tell is the shared, singular pledged asset.

c3_d4.t: A fraudster presents falsified shipping documents to draw payment under a genuine letter of credit. Separately, a fraudster creates an entirely fake letter of credit to support a loan application. These are, respectively:
o: Documentary (falsified-documents) LC fraud and fictitious LC fraud
Fictitious LC fraud and documentary LC fraud
c3_d4.e: Presenting falsified documents under a real LC is documentary LC fraud; fabricating a non-existent LC is fictitious LC fraud. The discriminator is whether the LC itself is genuine (documents faked) or wholly invented.

c3_j4.t: An examiner reviews a suspected inside/outside fraud. Why is this category generally the HARDEST to detect?
o: It involves the largest sums by definition
It only occurs at small institutions
An insider with legitimate access lends knowledge and authority to conceal an outsider's actions, defeating controls designed for one or the other alone
c3_j4.e: Inside/outside frauds pair an insider's legitimate access and system knowledge with an outsider's actions, so controls built to stop a lone insider or a lone outsider are individually circumvented. Sum size (A) varies; it occurs at institutions of all sizes (B); and it does leave a trail, just a concealed one (C).

c3_j5.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support an allegation of loan fraud?
o: A borrower's business genuinely failed after an honest, fully documented application and a market downturn
A borrower's listed employer's phone routes to the loan officer's own voicemail
A borrower pledged the same warehouse to three lenders
A borrower's stated income on the application is contradicted by verified tax records
c3_j5.e: An honest, fully documented application followed by a genuine market-driven failure is a credit loss, not fraud — there is no misrepresentation. The others show falsified income (D), double-pledging (C), and a fabricated employer (B). 'LEAST support' rewards isolating the case with no deception.

c4_j1.t: A retailer wants the MOST effective control to prevent skimming of unrecorded cash sales at the point of sale. Which is best?
o: Daily manager review of the general ledger
A visible, enforced policy pairing each sale with a mandatory customer receipt, combined with independent reconciliation of till counts to expected sales from inventory movement
c4_j1.e: Skimming leaves no book entry, so ledger review (A) and bank reconciliation (C) — which examine recorded figures — cannot see it. The defence attacks the point of theft: forcing a receipt for every sale removes the 'no record' option, and reconciling cash to inventory depletion catches sales that produced no recorded revenue. An annual audit (B) is far too infrequent and sample-based.

c4_j2.t: An examiner suspects lapping in accounts receivable. Which procedure is MOST diagnostic?
o: Confirming the total receivables balance with the general ledger
Comparing the dates and amounts customers say they paid against the dates those payments were posted to their accounts
c4_j2.e: Lapping is exposed by the lag between when a customer paid and when their account was credited — because the fraudster covers A with B's later money, postings drift behind actual payment dates. Direct customer confirmation of payment dates versus posting dates surfaces it. Agreeing totals (C) is useless since lapping keeps the total roughly intact. Bad-debt (A) and credit policy (B) are unrelated.

c4_d1.t: Employee X pockets cash from a sale and never rings it into the register. Employee Y rings the sale correctly, then removes the cash from the drawer at end of shift, leaving the till short. These are, respectively:
c4_d1.e: X takes the money before any record exists = skimming (off-book, no discrepancy created). Y takes it after the sale was recorded = cash larceny (the recorded total now exceeds the drawer). The single discriminator is whether the sale was entered before the cash left.

c4_d2.t: A cashier removes cash after ringing sales, then processes false refunds to reduce the recorded sales total so the register reconciles. Separately, a clerk records a $100 sale as $60 and keeps $40. These are, respectively:
o: Cash larceny concealed by false refunds and understated-sales skimming
Understated-sales skimming and larceny concealed by false refunds
c4_d2.e: The first employee recorded the sales, then stole and used false refunds to erase the resulting discrepancy — larceny with a concealment tool. The second never recorded the full amount — understated-sales skimming (off-book from the start). Watch the trap: a false refund follows a recorded sale, so it is a larceny-concealment device, not skimming.

c4_d3.t: Scheme 1: an employee intercepts a customer's mailed cheque and covers the missing payment using a later customer's cheque. Scheme 2: an employee removes cash from the day's bank deposit and uses the next day's deposit to cover it. These are, respectively:
c4_d3.e: Scheme 1 steals an incoming payment before it is posted and rolls it forward — receivables lapping, a skimming technique. Scheme 2 steals from a recorded deposit and rolls it forward — deposit lapping, a larceny technique. Both 'lap', but one is pre-record (skimming) and one is post-record (larceny).

c4_s1.scenario: A wholesale distributor's accounts-receivable clerk handles both incoming customer cheques and the posting of those payments to customer accounts. Over several months, customers begin complaining that payments they made are showing as overdue. Investigation finds that Customer A's March payment was posted on 12 April using funds that arrived from Customer B, whose own payment was then covered by Customer C's later remittance. The receivables total ties to the ledger throughout. The clerk took no holidays during the period and resisted attempts to have anyone cover their desk.
o: Fraudulent disbursement via a shell company
c4_s1.e: Payments posted late using the next customer's money, a total that stays intact, and a clerk who controls both receipting and posting and never lets anyone cover — these are the textbook markers of lapping. It is skimming because the theft occurs as payments come in, before correct posting. Larceny (A) would show a deposit discrepancy; the total here is preserved. Not FSF (B) or disbursement fraud (C).

c4_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which single control would have been MOST effective at preventing this scheme?
o: Segregating the handling of incoming payments from the posting of those payments to customer accounts, and enforcing mandatory rotation/leave
Requiring the clerk to reconcile the bank account monthly
c4_s2.e: Lapping requires one person to both receive payments and control their posting. Segregating those duties removes the ability to misdirect a payment and conceal it, and mandatory leave/rotation forces exposure (the scheme collapses the moment someone else posts). Having the same clerk reconcile (D) preserves the conflict. Reserves (A) and less-frequent statements (C) do nothing or make it worse.

c4_s3.scenario: A café's owner notices that one cashier's shifts consistently show lower cash-to-sales ratios than other cashiers working the same hours. The point-of-sale data shows this cashier processes a markedly higher number of 'no sale' drawer opens and post-transaction voids than peers. End-of-shift drawer counts for this cashier occasionally come up short, but on most days reconcile exactly. Inventory of high-margin items depletes faster than recorded sales of those items would imply.
c4_s3.t: Which combination of schemes is MOST consistent with the full pattern?
o: Both skimming (unrecorded/understated sales, shown by inventory depletion without sales) and cash larceny (shown by shortages, excessive voids and 'no sale' opens)
c4_s3.e: Two signatures coexist. Inventory depleting faster than recorded sales indicates sales that were never fully recorded — skimming. Drawer shortages plus abnormal voids and 'no sale' opens indicate cash removed after recording, with voids used to mask it — cash larceny. The 'reconciles exactly on most days' detail fits voids being used to bridge discrepancies. A and C each capture only half.

c4_j3.t: Why is skimming generally HARDER to detect than cash larceny?
o: Skimming produces no direct book entry, so there is no recorded discrepancy to find; larceny creates a record-to-cash mismatch
Skimming is not actually a crime
Larceny is always committed by managers
c4_j3.e: Cash larceny leaves a discrepancy between the record and the cash — a trail to follow. Skimming is off-book: the money never entered the records, so there is nothing to reconcile against, and detection needs indirect methods (invigilation, ratio and inventory analysis). Amounts (B) and perpetrator level (D) are not the reason; D is false.

c4_d4.t: An employee conceals skimmed receivables by writing the customer's balance off as uncollectible. A different employee conceals register cash theft by voiding legitimate sales after the fact. These concealment methods are associated, respectively, with:
c4_d4.e: A write-off of a receivable hides a pre-recording theft of an incoming payment = skimming concealment. A post-hoc void of a recorded sale hides cash removed after recording = larceny concealment. Match the concealment to whether the underlying theft was off-book (skimming) or on-book (larceny).

c4_j4.t: An analyst reviews a cashier with frequent voids. Which additional fact would MOST strengthen a larceny hypothesis rather than an innocent explanation?
o: The voids cluster near shift-end and correspond to drawer shortages of similar magnitude
The cashier is new and still learning the system
Voids require a supervisor code the cashier does not have
The store is busy and errors are common
c4_j4.e: Voids that cluster at shift-end and match the size of drawer shortages tie the voids to concealment of removed cash — the hallmark of larceny with false-void cover. A new cashier (B) and a busy store (D) are innocent explanations. If voids need a supervisor code the cashier lacks (C), it actually weakens the hypothesis that this cashier is voiding to conceal.

c4_j5.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support an allegation of a cash-receipts scheme?
o: A documented, approved seasonal discount reduced recorded sales, with cash and inventory fully reconciling
Sales revenue is flat while foot traffic and inventory depletion rise
One cashier has far more refunds and shortages than peers
Customer payments are consistently posted days after the customers say they paid
c4_j5.e: A documented, approved discount that fully reconciles to cash and inventory is legitimate — recorded sales fell for an authorised reason with no missing cash or stock. The others signal skimming (A: sales lag traffic/inventory), larceny (B: shortages and refunds), and lapping (D: posting lag). 'LEAST support' rewards isolating the fully reconciled, authorised case.

c5_j1.t: A warehouse operation wants the MOST effective control to detect ongoing inventory theft concealed by fraudulent write-offs. Which is best?
o: Independent periodic physical counts reconciled to perpetual records, plus review of write-off/adjustment volume and authorisation by someone without inventory custody
c5_j1.e: Theft hidden by write-offs is caught by independent physical counts against the perpetual record and scrutiny of who authorises write-offs — the concealment only works while the write-off approver also controls the stock. Insurance (B) transfers loss, it does not detect fraud. Reorder frequency (A) and lighting (C) do not reveal record manipulation.

c5_j2.t: An examiner observes steadily rising inventory shrinkage at one distribution centre. Which analysis would MOST effectively distinguish theft from legitimate causes?
o: Comparing shrinkage trends by product, shift, and employee, and cross-referencing spikes with write-off and adjustment activity
c5_j2.e: Legitimate shrinkage (breakage, spoilage, miscounts) is broadly distributed; theft concentrates by location, shift, or employee and correlates with unusual write-offs. Segmented trend analysis surfaces that concentration. Depreciation (C), dividends (D), and bank balances (B) are unrelated to physical inventory loss.

c5_d1.t: Employee A takes the company's portable generator home each weekend and returns it Monday. Employee B loads pallets of product onto a truck and sells them, writing the goods off as 'damaged'. These are, respectively:
c5_d1.e: A returns the asset — unauthorised misuse. B permanently removes the goods and conceals via write-off — theft. The discriminator is whether the asset comes back. Misuse is costed differently and treated as the lesser scheme, though it can escalate to theft.

c5_d2.t: Scheme 1: a receiving clerk marks incoming goods as 'short-shipped' and diverts the unrecorded units. Scheme 2: a sales clerk generates a fake shipping document so goods leave the warehouse as a 'sale' that is later written off as a bad debt. These are, respectively:
o: False shipment scheme and receiving scheme
Receiving (false receiving report) scheme and false shipment scheme
c5_d2.e: Scheme 1 falsifies the receiving report so stolen goods were never booked as received. Scheme 2 fabricates a shipment/sale so goods leave as if sold, then buries the receivable in a write-off. One manipulates the inbound record, the other the outbound record.

c5_d3.t: An employee simply carries finished goods out of the stockroom with no record manipulation at all. A different employee steals goods and reclassifies them in the system as obsolete scrap. The concealment sophistication differs; the schemes are, respectively:
o: Larceny (unconcealed) and theft concealed by fraudulent write-off
c5_d3.e: The first is straightforward larceny with no record cover — the asset just goes missing and shows as shrinkage. The second uses a fraudulent write-off (scrap/obsolete) to make the theft disappear from the books. Same underlying theft; different concealment sophistication, which is what the question tests.

c5_s1.scenario: A manufacturer's cost accountant reviews a plant where gross margin has quietly eroded over 18 months despite stable selling prices and input costs. Perpetual inventory records reconcile to the physical counts each quarter. However, the plant's 'scrap and obsolescence' write-offs have tripled, are almost always authorised by the same shift supervisor, and spike in the days immediately before each quarterly count. The supervisor both approves write-offs and has custody of the finished-goods store. Local scrap dealers have no record of receiving the volumes written off.
o: Inventory theft concealed by fraudulent scrap/obsolescence write-offs, timed to make counts reconcile
A pricing error in the cost system
Cash larceny at the point of sale
Legitimate obsolescence in a declining product line
c5_s1.e: The counts reconcile because the write-offs are timed just before each count to erase the missing stock from the book figure. Tripled write-offs, single-approver, custody-and-approval in one person, pre-count timing, and scrap that never reached any dealer point squarely to theft concealed by false write-offs. Genuine obsolescence (D) would not vanish before dealers and would not correlate with one supervisor. Not a pricing error (B) or cash scheme (C).

c5_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which control weakness was the PRIMARY enabler of the scheme?
o: Gross margin was not reviewed often enough
The plant used quarterly rather than monthly counts
The scrap dealers kept poor records
The same person both authorised write-offs and had custody of the inventory
c5_s2.e: The scheme depended on one person controlling both custody of the stock and authorisation of its write-off — a segregation-of-duties failure that let theft be disguised as approved scrap. Count frequency (B) and margin review cadence (A) are detective timing issues, not the root enabler. The dealers' records (C) were a detection aid, not the cause.

c5_j3.t: Which measure would be LEAST effective at preventing theft of inventory by employees with custody of it?
o: Independent physical counts by staff without custody
Analytical review of shrinkage and write-off trends
Segregating custody from record-keeping and write-off authorisation
A well-publicised code of ethics poster in the break room
c5_j3.e: An ethics poster has negligible preventive effect against an employee already stealing with custodial access. The genuinely effective controls are segregation of duties (C), independent counts (A), and analytical review (B). 'LEAST effective' rewards spotting the token control among substantive ones.

c5_j4.t: An examiner finds that recorded cost of goods sold has risen faster than sales, with no change in supplier pricing. What does this MOST likely indicate, and what should be done next?
o: Possible unrecorded inventory theft flowing through COGS; investigate shrinkage, write-offs and physical counts by location
c5_j4.e: COGS rising faster than sales with stable input prices signals inventory leaving without corresponding revenue — a classic analytical symptom of inventory theft. The next step is to drill into shrinkage, write-offs, and counts by location to localise it. It is not a marketing (B) or tax (A) issue, and it is not normal (C) given the stable-price condition.

c5_d4.t: An employee steals a competitor-sensitive customer database. Another employee steals physical laptops from a storeroom. In misappropriation terms these are, respectively:
o: Theft of tangible assets and misappropriation of intangible assets
Misappropriation of intangible assets and theft of tangible assets
c5_d4.e: A customer database is an intangible asset — its theft is misappropriation of intangibles (overlapping the IP/data-theft chapter). The laptops are tangible assets — ordinary theft of inventory/other assets. The discriminator is physical versus non-physical property.

c6_d1.t: A blank cheque is stolen from a company chequebook and the CFO's signature is imitated. Separately, a cheque validly signed by the CFO and payable to a supplier is stolen from the mail and the supplier's signature is imitated on the back. These are, respectively:
c6_d1.e: First: the drawer's (CFO's) signature is forged = forged maker. Second: the cheque was genuinely drawn, but the payee's (supplier's) signature is forged = forged endorsement. The discriminator is whose signature is faked — the maker or the payee.

c6_d2.t: A genuine cheque signed by the drawer has its payee name and amount altered after signing. A separate cheque is entirely manufactured on a home printer using a real account number. These are, respectively:
c6_d2.e: Changing the payee/amount on a genuine signed cheque = altered cheque. Fabricating the instrument itself = counterfeit cheque. One tampers with a real cheque; the other creates a fake one from scratch.

c6_j1.t: A bank wants the MOST diagnostic single indicator to flag cheque kiting on a business account. Which should it monitor?
o: Whether the account holder visits the branch
Whether average daily float substantially exceeds the average ledger balance, with matched deposits/withdrawals between the same set of accounts
The total number of cheques written per month
c6_j1.e: Kiting runs on float, not real money: when average daily float dwarfs the ledger balance, and deposits/withdrawals pair up between the same accounts with escalating amounts, the account is operating on uncollected funds. Cheque volume alone (C), opening balance (D), and branch visits (A) are not diagnostic of the float exploitation.

c6_j2.t: An accounts-payable team receives an email, apparently from a known supplier, requesting that future payments go to a new bank account. Which control MOST effectively prevents a business-email-compromise loss?
o: Confirming the change by replying to the same email thread
Verifying the account-change request out-of-band using contact details already on file, not those in the request
Requiring the email to be marked 'urgent' before acting
c6_j2.e: BEC often comes from a genuinely compromised or convincingly spoofed address, so replying in-thread (A) reaches the fraudster. The effective control is out-of-band verification using independently held contact details for any change of banking instructions. Urgency (D) is a fraudster's lever, not a control; encryption (C) protects data at rest, not this social-engineering vector.

c6_d3.t: A fraudster changes a cardholder's registered address, then reports the card lost so a replacement ships to the new address. Separately, a genuinely issued replacement card is intercepted from the victim's mailbox before it ever reaches them. These are, respectively:
c6_d3.e: Seizing an existing account by changing details and requesting a replacement = account takeover. Intercepting a genuinely issued card in transit, with no takeover = never-received issue (NRI). The discriminator is whether the fraudster manipulated the existing account (takeover) or merely stole a card in the mail (NRI).

c6_s1.scenario: A small distributor holds current accounts at Bank North and Bank South. A fraud analyst at Bank North reviews the account after a teller notices unusual patterns. Each Monday the distributor deposits into Bank North a cheque drawn on Bank South; each Tuesday it deposits into Bank South a cheque drawn on Bank North. The paired amounts are close but each week slightly larger than the last. Neither account holds meaningful collected funds at any point; the balances shown are almost entirely uncollected deposits. The account holder telephones both banks frequently to ask the current available balance.
c6_s1.e: Matched round-trip cheques between two banks, drawn against uncollected funds, with escalating amounts and frequent balance enquiries, and balances made up almost entirely of float — this is cheque kiting. The fraud is the exploitation of the collection-time gap. None of the card or endorsement schemes fit a two-bank float pattern.

c6_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which change by the banks would MOST directly collapse the scheme?
o: Offering the customer a credit card
Shortening the funds-availability (hold) period so deposits must clear before withdrawal
Sending the customer paper statements more often
c6_s2.e: Kiting survives only while float exists — the delay between deposit and collection. Shortening the availability period forces deposits to clear before funds can be drawn, eliminating the float the scheme runs on. Raising the overdraft (B) or issuing credit (A) hands the fraudster more room; statement frequency (D) is detective, not preventive.

c6_d4.t: A complicit merchant runs an unlicensed operator's card transactions through its own merchant account for a fee. Separately, a fraudster runs many tiny test charges on stolen card numbers to see which still work before a big purchase. These are, respectively:
c6_d4.e: Laundering another's transactions through a legitimate merchant account = factoring. Testing stolen numbers with small charges = carding. One monetises processing access; the other validates stolen data before exploitation.

c6_j3.t: Which statement about cryptocurrency is MOST accurate for a fraud examiner tracing illicit funds?
o: Transactions can always be reversed by the exchange
It is pseudonymous and irreversible; the ledger is public and traceable, with the best investigative leverage at exchange on/off ramps where identity is verified
It is fully anonymous and cannot be traced
It cannot be used in laundering because it is regulated
c6_j3.e: Crypto is pseudonymous, not anonymous: the blockchain is a permanent public ledger, transactions are irreversible, and the practical point to link a wallet to a person is the KYC-verified exchange on/off ramp. It is not untraceable (C), not reversible by exchanges after the fact (A), and its irreversibility and cross-border reach make it attractive for laundering (D).

c6_j4.t: A cardholder built a spotless payment history over a year, then within a week maxed every credit line and became unreachable. This is BEST described as, and MOST resembles which other scheme?
o: A bust-out; resembles the bankruptcy bust-out where built-up credit is deliberately exhausted before disappearing
c6_j4.e: A bust-out spends the creditworthiness patiently built — the clean history is the investment phase. It mirrors the bankruptcy bust-out, where a business builds credit, loads up, and then defaults or files. The others do not match the build-then-exhaust pattern.

c6_j5.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support an allegation of cheque kiting?
o: Matched cheques cycle between two banks with escalating amounts
The account holder phones daily to check the available balance
A single large cheque is deposited and clears normally against genuine collected funds
Average daily float vastly exceeds the ledger balance
c6_j5.e: A single cheque clearing against genuine collected funds is ordinary banking — no float exploitation, no cycling. The others are classic kiting signatures: matched inter-bank cycling (A), float exceeding ledger balance (D), and obsessive balance checking (B). 'LEAST support' rewards isolating the legitimate transaction.

c7_d1.t: Specifications for a tender are written to match one vendor's proprietary product so closely that no other supplier can qualify. Separately, during evaluation a corrupt officer manipulates the scoring to favour a bidder. These occur, respectively, in which phases and are called what?
o: Presolicitation/bid tailoring and evaluation/bid rigging (corrupt evaluation)
c7_d1.e: Writing exclusionary specs occurs in the presolicitation phase = bid tailoring. Manipulating scoring occurs in the evaluation phase = bid rigging / corrupt evaluation. The exam distinguishes these primarily by phase — before the tender versus during evaluation.

c7_d2.t: Four contractors agree that each will submit deliberately high bids on jobs assigned to the others, so the designated winner appears to have won competitively. In a different ring, competitors simply agree not to bid against whoever is 'up' next. These are, respectively:
c7_d2.e: Submitting deliberately high cover bids to fake competition = complementary bidding. Agreeing not to bid at all = bid suppression. Both are collusion, but one manufactures the appearance of competition while the other removes competitors entirely.

c7_d3.t: A supplier delivers grade-B components while invoicing for the specified grade-A. A different contractor wins with an unusually low bid, then recovers its margin through a stream of inflated change orders. These are, respectively:
c7_d3.e: Delivering lower-grade goods while billing for the specified grade = product substitution. Winning low then recovering through inflated changes = change-order abuse (tell: low bid + abnormal change volume). Both are post-award, but the mechanisms are distinct.

c7_j1.t: An auditor analysing years of tenders wants the MOST effective signal of collusive complementary bidding. Which should they examine?
o: Whether losing bids cluster at a consistent margin above the winner and whether the winner rotates among the same small set of firms
The number of pages in each bid
The absolute size of the winning bids
c7_j1.e: Genuine competitors' estimates scatter; colluders' losing bids sit at a consistent margin above the winner, with the winner rotating among the same firms — a statistical fingerprint. Bid size (D), page count (C), and payment terms (A) carry no collusion signal.

c7_j2.t: A government official awards a contract to a company secretly owned by their sibling. The price was fair and no payment passed to the official. Is there a violation, and why?
o: No, because the sibling, not the official, benefited
Yes — a conflict of interest is complete upon the undisclosed interest, regardless of fair pricing or absence of payment
No, because the price was fair and no bribe was paid
Only if the contract later underperformed
c7_j2.e: A conflict of interest requires only the undisclosed interest; it needs no bribe, no loss, and no unfair price. Fair pricing (C) and the benefit accruing to a relative (A) do not cure the non-disclosure, and outcome (D) is irrelevant. This is the distinction from bribery, which requires a corrupt payment.

c7_s1.scenario: An oversight body reviews eleven road-maintenance contracts awarded by a municipality over three years. The same four construction firms bid on every tender. The winner rotates in a near-perfect cycle. The losing bids sit consistently 18–22% above the winning bid on every contract. Metadata in one losing firm's electronic bid document shows it was created on a computer registered to the eventual winner. No firm outside the four ever submitted a bid, though the region has many capable contractors.
c7_s1.t: The pattern MOST clearly evidences which combination of schemes?
o: Legitimate competition among four efficient firms
Complementary bidding combined with bid rotation (and evidence of bid preparation by a competitor)
c7_s1.e: A rotating winner, losing bids at a uniform 18–22% margin (statistically implausible among true competitors), only four firms bidding despite a deep market, and a losing bid authored on the winner's computer together establish complementary bidding plus bid rotation. Genuine competition (A) would show scattered margins and outside entrants. The post-award schemes (B) and a lone conflict (D) do not fit a multi-tender bidding pattern.

c7_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which single fact moved the case from statistical suspicion to direct evidence of collusion?
o: The winner rotated among the firms
A losing bid document was created on a computer registered to the winner
Losing bids clustered at 18–22% above the winner
c7_s2.e: The rotation, the uniform margins, and the closed field are powerful statistical indicators, but each could in theory have an innocent explanation. A losing bid physically prepared on the winner's computer is direct evidence that the 'competing' bids were coordinated. The statistical patterns (A, D, B) build suspicion; the document metadata proves it.

c7_d4.t: A contractor on a cost-plus government contract charges to it costs actually incurred on a separate fixed-price job. A different contractor submits pricing data it knows is outdated to inflate a negotiated contract price. These are, respectively:
c7_d4.e: Shifting costs onto the contract that reimburses them (cost-plus) = cost mischarging. Submitting non-current/inaccurate cost or pricing data to inflate a negotiated price = defective pricing. One misallocates real costs; the other misrepresents the cost data itself.

c7_j3.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support an allegation of procurement fraud?
o: Technical specifications precisely match one vendor's proprietary catalogue
A competitive open tender attracted many outside bidders, with scattered bid margins and a documented, justified award to the lowest qualified bid
The evaluating official held an undisclosed stake in the winning firm
The winning bid was abnormally low, followed by many inflated change orders
c7_j3.e: An open tender with many bidders, naturally scattered margins, and a documented lowest-qualified award is the picture of legitimate competition. The others show bid tailoring (A), change-order abuse (D), and an undisclosed conflict (C). 'LEAST support' rewards isolating the transparent, competitive process.

c7_j4.t: A public agency wants the MOST effective control to prevent need-recognition and bid-tailoring fraud at the earliest procurement phase. Which is best?
o: Publishing the winning bid amount after award
Requiring bidders to post a performance bond
Independent review of the justification of need and of specifications for restrictive, vendor-specific requirements before the tender is issued
Awarding all contracts to the lowest bidder automatically
c7_j4.e: Need-recognition and bid-tailoring occur in presolicitation, so the control must act before the tender issues: independent review of the stated need and of specs for vendor-lock-in language. Auto-lowest-bid (D) ignores tailored specs; post-award publication (A) is too late; a performance bond (B) addresses delivery risk, not specification manipulation.

c8_j1.t: An analyst has one procedure to screen for revenue-recognition fraud across a portfolio of companies. Which is MOST diagnostic?
o: Comparing the growth of revenue against the growth of operating cash flow and receivables over the same periods
Checking that the balance sheet balances
Confirming the audit opinion was unqualified
c8_j1.e: Fictitious or prematurely recognised revenue does not convert to cash — it accumulates as receivables, so revenue outpacing operating cash flow and receivables ballooning faster than sales is the strongest single screen. A clean opinion gives only reasonable assurance and is not diagnostic. EPS and a balancing balance sheet are trivially satisfied even amid fraud.

c8_j2.t: Which analytical technique BEST reveals that cost of goods sold was manipulated relative to sales across three years?
o: Confirming the cash balance with the bank
Vertical (common-size) analysis expressing each line as a percentage of sales
c8_j2.e: Vertical (common-size) analysis states each income-statement line as a percent of sales, making an abnormal COGS-to-sales shift immediately visible across periods. A bank reconciliation, custody review, and cash confirmation address other risks entirely and cannot surface a margin manipulation.

c8_d1.t: Company A records genuine December sales in November to hit a quarterly target. Company B books sales to a customer that does not exist. These are, respectively:
o: A timing difference and fictitious revenue
Fictitious revenue and a timing difference
c8_d1.e: Recording a real sale in the wrong period = timing difference. Booking a sale to a non-existent customer = fictitious revenue. The discriminator is whether the sale is real-but-mistimed or wholly fabricated.

c8_d2.t: Company A fails to record a known warranty reserve. Company B omits from its notes a material lawsuit filed after year-end. These are, respectively:
o: Concealed liabilities/expenses and improper disclosure (subsequent events)
c8_d2.e: Omitting a required reserve understates recorded obligations = concealed liabilities. Omitting a material post-year-end event from the notes = improper disclosure (subsequent events). One misstates a number on the face; the other hides truth in the footnotes.

c8_d3.t: Company A ships product to a distributor with an unconditional right of return near period-end and books it all as revenue. Company B capitalises routine repair costs as fixed assets. These are, respectively:
o: Improper asset valuation and timing difference
A timing difference (channel stuffing) and concealed expense (improper capitalisation)
c8_d3.e: Booking returnable product to hit the quarter is channel stuffing — a timing/premature-revenue scheme. Capitalising an operating cost defers the expense off the income statement — a concealed expense that overstates both assets and income.

c8_s1.scenario: A public company reports 40% revenue growth for the year, yet operating cash flow is roughly flat. Accounts receivable rose 95% and days-sales-outstanding nearly doubled. A large share of the fourth-quarter revenue came from three new distributors, each granted extended payment terms and a right to return unsold goods. In the first quarter of the following year, those distributors returned significant volumes. Inventory at the distributors was well above their historical sell-through.
o: Channel stuffing — premature revenue recognition on returnable goods
c8_s1.e: Revenue surging while cash flow stays flat, DSO doubling, quarter-end sales to new distributors with return rights, and heavy Q1 returns are the classic markers of channel stuffing — recognising revenue on goods likely to come back. Genuine growth converts to cash. There is no tax or capitalisation element in the facts.

c8_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which single metric most economically exposed the scheme before the returns occurred?
o: The widening gap between revenue growth and operating cash flow, corroborated by rising days-sales-outstanding
c8_s2.e: The revenue-to-cash-flow divergence plus rising DSO flagged the problem in real time — fictitious or premature revenue accumulates as uncollected receivables rather than cash. EPS and the audit opinion lag and can look fine; the dividend ratio is unrelated.

c8_s3.scenario: A manufacturer under earnings pressure reports improved net income. An examiner notes that the fixed-asset ledger grew sharply, with numerous additions individually below the capitalisation threshold review level, described as 'plant improvements'. On inspection, many of these were routine maintenance and repair jobs — replacing worn belts, repainting, servicing machinery — that historically had been expensed. Repair-and-maintenance expense on the income statement fell to a fraction of prior years despite an ageing asset base.
c8_s3.t: The scheme and its effect on the financial statements are:
o: Improper capitalisation of expenses; overstating both assets and net income
Improper disclosure; hiding a related party
Timing difference; shifting revenue between periods
c8_s3.e: Recording routine repairs as capital 'improvements' is improper capitalisation. Deferring the expense off the income statement overstates net income and overstates assets simultaneously — the two-part effect the exam tests. The collapse in repair expense against an ageing asset base is the tell.

c8_j3.t: Which of the following would LEAST support an allegation of financial statement fraud?
o: A dominant CEO routinely overrides accounting controls
Receivables grow much faster than sales
Stable, growing operating cash flow comfortably funds a consistent dividend
Revenue grows far faster than operating cash flow year after year
c8_j3.e: Operating cash flow growing and funding dividends is a sign of financial health, not fraud — earnings are backed by cash. The others are classic FSF red flags: revenue outpacing cash, receivables outpacing sales, and control override. 'LEAST support' rewards isolating the healthy indicator.

c8_j4.t: At what point does aggressive-but-defensible accounting cross into financial statement fraud?
o: When the external auditor disagrees with a judgement
When estimates are used instead of exact figures
When the treatment reduces reported tax
When there is a material misstatement made with intent to deceive users who rely on the statements
c8_j4.e: The dividing line is material misstatement plus intent to deceive. Auditor disagreement, tax effects, and the use of estimates are ordinary features of financial reporting and do not, without materiality and intent, constitute fraud.

c8_d4.t: Company A over-accrues reserves in strong years and releases them in weak years to smooth earnings. Company B holds goods in its own warehouse but books them as sold because the customer was 'invoiced'. These are, respectively:
o: Cookie-jar reserves (improper accrual) and bill-and-hold (premature revenue)
Both timing differences of the same type
c8_d4.e: Building and releasing reserves to smooth results is a cookie-jar reserve scheme. Booking revenue while goods sit undelivered in the seller's warehouse is bill-and-hold — premature revenue because risk and delivery have not passed. Both distort periods, but through different mechanisms.

c9_d1.t: A vendor pays a purchasing manager before a contract is awarded, in exchange for selecting the vendor. Separately, a grateful vendor sends the manager an expensive watch after winning, with no prior arrangement. These are, respectively:
c9_d1.e: Payment before, to influence the award = bribery. A reward after, with no prior agreement = illegal gratuity. The single discriminator is timing/intent: was the payment agreed to influence a future decision, or given to reward a past one?

c9_d2.t: A purchasing agent demands a payment from a vendor, threatening to award the contract elsewhere if refused. Separately, a vendor offers a payment to persuade the agent to choose it. These are, respectively:
c9_d2.e: When the employee demands payment under threat = economic extortion (the coercive demand side). When the vendor offers payment to influence = bribery. Same money, opposite initiation — the exam distinguishes by who demanded versus who offered.

c9_d3.t: Vendor Sigma overbills a company by 50,000 and returns 20,000 to the manager who approved it. Separately, a manager awards a contract to a firm she secretly co-owns, disclosing nothing. These are, respectively:
o: A kickback (bribery variant) and an undisclosed conflict of interest
A conflict of interest and a kickback
c9_d3.e: A vendor returning part of an inflated payment to the employee who steered the business is a kickback (a bribery variant). An undisclosed ownership interest in a firm the manager selects is a conflict of interest — no payment needed; the undisclosed interest is the violation.

c9_j1.t: An official awards a contract to a company owned by his cousin. The price was competitive, no money passed to the official, and the work was satisfactory — but he never disclosed the relationship. Has a violation occurred, and why?
o: Only if the contract later underperformed
Yes — a conflict of interest is complete on the undisclosed interest, regardless of fair price or absence of payment
No, because the price was fair and no loss occurred
No, because the benefit went to a relative, not the official
c9_j1.e: A conflict of interest requires only the undisclosed interest. Fair pricing, absence of payment, a relative as beneficiary, and satisfactory performance do not cure the non-disclosure. The undisclosed divided loyalty is itself the violation — distinct from bribery, which requires a corrupt payment.

c9_j2.t: Which method is MOST effective for detecting corruption schemes, given that the underlying transactions often appear normal?
o: Tips combined with relationship and lifestyle analysis mapping employee-vendor connections
c9_j2.e: Corruption leaves little on the books — the invoice and payment can look ordinary. It is caught chiefly by tips and relationship/lifestyle analysis: employee-vendor links, unexplained wealth, and vendors winning against stronger competitors. Ledger totals, bank balances, and depreciation do not reveal a corrupt relationship.

c9_j3.t: A company wants the MOST effective preventive control against conflicts of interest in procurement. Which is best?
o: Mandatory periodic disclosure of employee financial and personal interests, with independent review and recusal
Increasing the number of bidders required
Awarding every contract to the lowest bidder
c9_j3.e: Since a conflict of interest is defined by non-disclosure, the control that attacks it directly is mandatory interest disclosure with independent review and recusal. Lowest-bidder rules, more bidders, and post-award publication do not surface an undisclosed personal interest before the decision is made.

c9_s1.scenario: An examiner reviews a mid-size manufacturer's purchasing. One buyer, over two years, shifted 70% of a commodity spend to a single mid-tier supplier that consistently beat stronger, cheaper competitors. Invoices from that supplier run 8–12% above market and are always approved by the same buyer without competitive quotes. The buyer recently purchased a car and a holiday home inconsistent with his salary. A corporate-registry search shows the supplier's registered office is the address of the buyer's spouse. None of this was disclosed.
o: An undisclosed conflict of interest, likely combined with kickbacks/overbilling
c9_s1.e: An undisclosed connection (spouse's address) to a favoured supplier, above-market pricing without competitive quotes, and unexplained lifestyle point to a conflict of interest, and the systematic overbilling suggests kickbacks flowing back. Sole-sourcing would be disclosed and justified. There is no threat/demand (extortion) or revenue element.

c9_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which fact most directly establishes the conflict of interest independent of any payment?
o: The supplier's registered office being the buyer's spouse's address, undisclosed
c9_s2.e: A conflict of interest is complete on the undisclosed personal interest itself — here, the buyer's family connection to the supplier, never disclosed. Pricing, lifestyle, and missing quotes evidence the associated kickback/overbilling, but the conflict is established by the undisclosed relationship regardless of any payment.

c9_d4.t: Three competitors agree that each will take a turn winning successive tenders. In a separate ring, competitors submit deliberately high bids so the chosen firm appears to win competitively. These are, respectively:
c9_d4.e: Taking turns as the designated winner = bid rotation. Submitting deliberately high losing bids to fake competition = complementary (cover) bidding. Both are collusion; one schedules the winner, the other manufactures the appearance of a contest.

c9_j4.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support an allegation of bribery (as opposed to another scheme or no offence)?
o: A buyer is paid to leak competitors' pricing before bids close
A vendor pays a manager before award to secure the contract
A manager receives a token holiday gift, openly disclosed and within an approved policy, after routine dealings
A vendor funds a manager's personal credit card in exchange for steering business
c9_j4.e: A token, openly disclosed gift within an approved policy, given after ordinary dealings with no agreement to influence, is not bribery — there is no corrupt intent to influence a decision. The others are clear bribery/kickback (pre-award payment, funded credit card, paid data leak). 'LEAST support' rewards isolating the disclosed, policy-compliant courtesy.

c10_d1.t: A launderer deposits illicit cash into several accounts in sub-threshold amounts. Later, the funds are wired through three offshore shell companies. These acts belong, respectively, to which stages?
c10_d1.e: Getting the cash into the system in sub-threshold deposits = placement (via structuring). Moving it through offshore shells to obscure origin = layering. The order is entry-first, obscuring-movement-second.

c10_d2.t: After layering, laundered funds are used to buy a hotel that operates as a genuine business. Separately, dirty cash is mixed with real receipts inside a launderette the launderer owns. These illustrate, respectively:
o: Integration (legitimate-asset acquisition) and placement/integration via a cash-intensive front
c10_d2.e: Buying a genuine operating business with laundered money is integration — the funds re-enter as legitimate wealth. Mixing illicit cash with real takings in a cash-intensive front both places the cash and integrates it under cover of legitimate revenue. Both concern making dirty money look clean, not merely moving it.

c10_j1.t: A compliance analyst must decide whether a pattern of deposits constitutes structuring. Which fact is MOST determinative?
o: Whether the customer is a business or individual
Whether the deposits were in cash or cheque
Evidence that the deposits were deliberately kept below the reporting threshold to avoid a report being filed
The total amount deposited over the period
c10_j1.e: Structuring turns on intent to evade the reporting threshold — deliberately keeping deposits below the trigger to prevent a report. The total amount, customer type, and instrument are context; none establishes the offence. Structuring is illegal even when the cash is from a legal source, precisely because of that evasive intent.

c10_j2.t: Which statement about structuring is CORRECT?
o: It is only an offence if the underlying money is from crime
It requires moving funds across borders
It occurs only during the integration stage
It is an offence in itself even when the cash is from a legal source, because the intent is to defeat reporting
c10_j2.e: Structuring is independently unlawful regardless of the money's origin — the wrong is the deliberate evasion of the reporting requirement. It does not require cross-border movement and is a placement-stage technique, not integration.

c10_j3.t: Which international body issues the 40 Recommendations that form the global AML/CFT standard?
o: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision
c10_j3.e: FATF issues the 40 Recommendations — the international AML/CFT benchmark. The Basel Committee sets prudential (not AML) standards, the Egmont Group links national FIUs, and Wolfsberg issues private-banking AML principles.

c10_s1.scenario: A bank's monitoring flags a customer who, over six weeks, made 41 cash deposits across four branches, each between 8,000 and 9,500, on 22 different days. The customer's stated occupation is a small retail trader whose declared turnover cannot support these volumes. Shortly after each cluster of deposits, funds were wired to a company in another jurisdiction and then onward to two further entities. The customer became agitated when a teller mentioned that large cash deposits are reported.
c10_s1.t: Which combination is MOST clearly evidenced?
c10_s1.e: Many sub-threshold cash deposits across branches and days, inconsistent with declared turnover, plus agitation at the mention of reporting, are the signature of structuring at the placement stage. The subsequent onward wires through multiple entities are layering. It is not kiting (no matched inter-bank float scheme) and involves more than integration alone.

c10_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which fact most directly supports an inference of intent to evade reporting?
o: The customer is a retail trader
Deposits were consistently kept just below the reporting threshold, spread across branches and days, with visible concern at the mention of reporting
c10_s2.e: Intent to evade is inferred from deposits deliberately kept just under the threshold, dispersed across branches and days, coupled with the customer's reaction to the reporting reference. Being a trader, wiring abroad, and using cash are consistent with the scheme but do not, alone, establish the evasive intent that defines structuring.

c10_d3.t: A launderer over-invoices an export shipment to move value abroad under cover of trade. Separately, a launderer runs many small transactions through a mixing service to break the crypto audit trail. These are, respectively:
c10_d3.e: Over-/under-invoicing trade to move value = trade-based laundering. Running funds through a mixer to obscure the crypto trail = layering. Both obscure origin/value movement, but through different vehicles — trade documents versus blockchain mixing.

c10_j4.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support a suspicion of money laundering?
o: A cash-intensive business deposits receipts far exceeding its plausible customer volume
A registered business deposits daily takings consistent with its declared, verifiable turnover and audited accounts
A customer structures deposits just below the reporting threshold across several branches
Funds are rapidly moved through several shell companies with no economic purpose
c10_j4.e: A business whose deposits match its declared, verifiable, audited turnover shows a normal, explainable cash flow — no laundering indicator. The others are classic red flags: implausible cash volumes (front business), structuring, and purposeless movement through shells (layering). 'LEAST support' rewards isolating the fully explained activity.

c11_j1.t: An investor is evaluating a fund. Which single characteristic is the STRONGEST indicator of a Ponzi scheme?
o: The fund reports quarterly rather than monthly
The manager holds a professional licence
The fund invests in listed equities
Returns are consistently smooth and positive across all market conditions, with assets self-custodied and no independent auditor
c11_j1.e: Real markets are volatile. Implausibly smooth returns regardless of conditions, combined with self-custody and no independent auditor, indicates returns are manufactured rather than earned — nobody independent verifies the assets exist. Listed investments, a licence, and reporting frequency are neutral.

c11_d1.t: Scheme A pays passive investors monthly 'returns' funded entirely from new subscriptions. Scheme B pays investors only if they each enrol two more participants. These are, respectively:
c11_d1.e: Ponzi = passive investors paid from later investors' principal. Pyramid = payout depends on the investor's own recruitment activity. The money mechanics can look similar; the classification turns on where the return is said to come from.

c11_d2.t: A broker with discretionary authority trades a client's account far more than the objectives warrant. A different broker trades its own book just before executing a large client order it knows will move the price. These are, respectively:
c11_d2.e: Churning = excessive trading in a controlled account to generate commissions. Front running = trading ahead of a known client order to profit from its price impact. One exploits commission; the other exploits order-flow knowledge.

c11_j2.t: For an insider trading allegation, which combination MUST be established?
o: The information was material AND non-public, and traded in breach of a duty
The trader was a company director AND a shareholder
The security was listed AND liquid
The trade was large and profitable
c11_j2.e: Both elements are required: information that is material (a reasonable investor would consider it important) and non-public, traded in breach of a duty. Non-public but trivial, or material but already public, fails. Trade size, profitability, role, and liquidity are not elements.

c11_s1.scenario: A promoter markets 'infrastructure bonds' promising 2.5% monthly returns with 'no downside risk'. Investors are passive; the promoter claims proprietary access to government contracts and declines to explain the strategy. For 19 months, every investor receives their stated return on time, including through a severe market downturn. Assets are held in accounts controlled by the promoter; there is no independent custodian or auditor. When several investors request redemption in the same month, payments stall and the promoter urges them to reinvest at a higher rate.
c11_s1.e: Passive investors, smooth returns through a downturn, opacity, self-custody with no independent verification, and collapse on concentrated redemptions are the definitive Ponzi markers — returns come from later investors' principal. There is no recruitment requirement (so not a pyramid), no non-public information trade, and no stock promotion.

c11_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which fact would MOST reliably have exposed the fraud before collapse?
o: Investors were passive rather than active
The promised return rate was high
Independent verification that the underlying assets and contracts actually existed, via a genuine custodian and auditor
c11_s2.e: Every other red flag is circumstantial; independent custody and audit would have tested whether the assets existed at all — the single fact a Ponzi cannot survive. High promised returns raise suspicion but are not proof; media reticence and investor passivity are weak signals.

c11_j3.t: What distinguishes an unlawful pyramid from a lawful multi-level marketing business?
o: Compensation flows chiefly from recruitment and inventory loading rather than genuine retail sales to end users
Lawful MLMs never charge an entry fee
c11_j3.e: Many pyramids include a nominal product as disguise. The test is where the money comes from: recruitment plus inventory loading (recruits forced to buy stock they cannot sell) is unlawful; genuine retail sales to end consumers is lawful. Geography and entry fees are not the discriminator.

c11_j4.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support a securities fraud allegation?
o: A broker over-trades a client account against the client's stated objectives
A promoter guarantees fixed high returns with no downside and self-custodies assets
A registered fund publishes audited results showing volatile returns tracking its stated benchmark, with independent custody
A promoter hypes a thinly traded stock then sells into the resulting demand
c11_j4.e: Volatile returns tracking a stated benchmark, independently audited and custodied is what genuine investment management looks like — variability is evidence of real market exposure. The others show a Ponzi profile, churning, and pump-and-dump. 'LEAST support' rewards spotting the legitimately verified fund.

c12_d1.t: Agent A persuades a client to replace an existing policy with a new one from the same insurer, purely to earn fresh commission. Agent B misrepresents facts to induce a client to move to a different insurer. These are, respectively:
c12_d1.e: Churning = replacement within the same insurer. Twisting = misrepresentation inducing a switch to another insurer. The discriminator is whether the insurer changes.

c12_d2.t: An agent collects premiums and never forwards them to the insurer. A different agent adds unrequested coverage to a client's policy and bills for it. These are, respectively:
c12_d2.e: Premium diversion = the agent keeps premium that should have gone to the insurer (the client believes they are covered but are not). Sliding = charging for coverage the client never agreed to. One steals the premium; the other manufactures extra charges.

c12_j1.t: Which combination of facts MOST strongly indicates arson for profit rather than accidental fire?
o: The fire occurred at night and the alarm failed
The business was in financial distress, the policy limit was substantially increased weeks earlier, and the fire had multiple unconnected points of origin
The building was old and the wiring outdated
The owner was away at the time
c12_j1.e: Arson for profit is established on the financial record plus physical impossibility: motive (distress), opportunity (recent over-insurance), and evidence incompatible with accident (multiple unconnected origin points cannot occur accidentally). Night, failed alarms, old wiring, and owner absence are all consistent with genuine accidents.

c12_j2.t: An employer understates its payroll and misclassifies high-risk workers into low-risk categories on its workers' compensation policy. Who is the perpetrator and what is the scheme?
c12_j2.e: Premium fraud is committed by the employer against the insurer, by misstating payroll, job classifications, or claims history to reduce premium. Note the perpetrator carefully — the exam frequently offers 'claimant fraud' as a distractor for what is actually an employer-side scheme.

c12_s1.scenario: An insurer's special investigations unit reviews 34 unrelated vehicle-injury claims filed over eight months. Although the claimants have no apparent connection to one another, 29 of the claims involve the same medical clinic, 26 list the same attorney, and the treatment course is near-identical: the same number of sessions, the same soft-tissue diagnoses, and similar billed amounts. Several claimants, when interviewed, say they were approached at the accident scene by a person who directed them to the clinic and lawyer. No claimant has objective imaging evidence of injury.
o: An organised insurance fraud ring using recruiters ('cappers'), a complicit provider and attorney
Coincidental use of a popular local clinic
c12_s1.e: The same clinic and attorney recurring across supposedly unrelated claims, identical treatment patterns, scene recruitment, and purely subjective injuries are the definitive markers of an organised ring — a capper recruits claimants, a complicit provider documents injuries, an attorney prosecutes them. Coincidence cannot explain identical treatment counts across 29 claims.

c12_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which analytical approach would MOST efficiently have surfaced this ring earlier?
o: Asking claimants to certify their claims
Reviewing each claim file individually for completeness
Increasing the deductible on all policies
Link analysis across claims to detect recurring providers, attorneys, and treatment patterns among unrelated claimants
c12_s2.e: Each individual file looked ordinary — which is why file-by-file review (and self-certification) fails. Link analysis across the claim population, detecting the same provider/attorney and identical treatment profiles among unrelated claimants, is what exposes an organised ring. Raising deductibles is a pricing lever, not a detection method.

c12_j3.t: Which single claim-level fact is the STRONGEST indicator of premeditated (rather than opportunistic) insurance fraud?
o: The claim was filed shortly after the policy was written or the limits were increased
c12_j3.e: A claim arriving shortly after inception or a limit increase suggests the coverage was procured for the loss — evidencing premeditation. Claim size, legal representation, and submission channel are all common in legitimate claims.

c12_j4.t: Which fact pattern would LEAST support an insurance fraud allegation?
o: An owner reports his vehicle stolen while being upside-down on the loan
A total-loss fire follows a doubling of coverage eight weeks earlier at a distressed business
The same clinic appears on dozens of unrelated injury claims
A claimant's injuries are documented by objective imaging, reported immediately with a police report, on a long-standing policy with no coverage changes
c12_j4.e: Objectively documented injuries, immediate reporting with a police report, and a long-standing policy with no recent changes describe an ordinary legitimate claim. The others show arson indicators, an organised ring, and a possible owner give-up. 'LEAST support' rewards isolating the corroborated, unremarkable claim.

c13_d1.t: Malware spreads across an entire corporate network overnight with no user present. Separately, an employee opens an email attachment and infects only his own machine. These are, respectively:
c13_d1.e: Self-propagation with no host file and no user action = worm. Requires a host file and user execution = virus. Overnight network-wide spread with nobody at their desk is the definitive worm signature.

c13_d2.t: Program A disguises itself as a legitimate utility and opens a backdoor once installed, but does not replicate. Program B lies dormant and begins deleting servers when its author's employee record disappears from payroll. These are, respectively:
o: A logic bomb and a Trojan horse
A Trojan horse and a logic bomb
c13_d2.e: A Trojan horse relies on disguise, not replication — the user installs it willingly. A logic bomb is dormant code triggered by a condition, here the author's own termination — the archetypal disgruntled-insider weapon.

c13_j1.t: Which statement about a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack is CORRECT?
o: It exfiltrates confidential data by overwhelming the server
It compromises availability rather than confidentiality; no data is stolen
It always installs ransomware on the target
It requires physical access to the target server
c13_j1.e: DDoS attacks availability — it denies service by exhausting capacity. It does not exfiltrate data. An option describing data theft via traffic flooding is wrong on the mechanism; DDoS also needs no physical access and does not inherently deploy ransomware.

c13_j2.t: Which measure would be LEAST effective against an insider with legitimate privileged access exfiltrating data?
o: Eliminating shared administrator accounts to preserve attribution
Logging and alerting on bulk data exports
Immediate revocation of privileged access upon notice of termination
A stronger external perimeter firewall and intrusion-detection system
c13_j2.e: An external firewall guards the perimeter and does nothing against someone already inside it with legitimate credentials. The effective insider controls are prompt access revocation, bulk-export monitoring, and eliminating shared admin accounts so actions can be attributed to individuals.

c13_j3.t: In practice, which is the MOST effective initial vector for gaining unauthorised access to an organisation's systems?
c13_j3.e: Social engineering remains dominant — technology is rarely the weak point; people are. This is why awareness training and verification procedures outperform most purely technical spending. Zero-days are rare and costly; brute force is largely defeated by lockouts; physical theft is uncommon.

c13_s1.scenario: A systems administrator is informed his role will be made redundant in 30 days. IT later discovers that during those 30 days he accessed servers outside his normal duties at unusual hours, used a shared 'admin' account for several actions, and committed code to a scheduled job. Nine days after his employment ended, production databases began deleting themselves. Forensic review shows the scheduled job checked nightly whether his employee ID still appeared in the HR system and, finding it absent, executed the deletions. His network credentials had never been revoked.
c13_s1.t: The scheme and the primary control failure are:
o: A logic bomb; failure to revoke privileged access at termination and use of shared admin accounts destroying attribution
c13_s1.e: Dormant code triggered by the condition of his ID vanishing from payroll is a logic bomb. The enabling failures were continuing privileged access after termination and shared admin accounts that obscured who did what. No encryption-for-ransom (ransomware), no self-propagation (worm), and no availability flooding (DDoS).

c13_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which control would have MOST directly prevented the loss?
o: Immediate revocation of all privileged access at notice of termination, combined with independent code review of scheduled jobs
c13_s2.e: The attack depended on retained privileged access and unreviewed code. Revoking access at notice and requiring independent review of scheduled jobs directly removes both. Password length is irrelevant to a legitimate credential holder; training does not deter a determined insider; budget alone is not a control.

c13_d3.t: Attacker A intercepts and can alter traffic passing between a user and a bank site. Attacker B diverts tiny rounding fractions from thousands of accounts into one account. These are, respectively:
o: A man-in-the-middle attack and the salami technique
The salami technique and a man-in-the-middle attack
c13_d3.e: Man-in-the-middle = interception (and possible alteration) of communications in transit. Salami technique = slicing amounts too small to be individually noticed, typically rounding fractions — invisible individually, substantial collectively.

c14_j1.t: A caller demands immediate payment of a supposed tax debt by gift card and insists the victim tell nobody. Which pairing of facts is the STRONGEST fraud indicator?
o: The demand for an irrevocable payment method combined with an appeal to secrecy
The call came outside business hours
The caller spoke quickly and had an accent
The call was unsolicited and the amount was large
c14_j1.e: Irrevocable payment (gift card, wire, crypto) plus enforced secrecy is the definitive signature. No revenue authority demands gift cards, and the secrecy exists solely to stop a bank teller or family member intervening. Unsolicited calls, accents, and timing are weak or prejudicial signals.

c14_j2.t: A victim of an earlier investment scam is telephoned by a 'recovery bureau' that knows the exact sum he lost and the name of the fraudulent firm. What does that knowledge MOST likely indicate?
o: The original firm has been prosecuted
The bureau is legitimate, since only genuine investigators would have those details
The caller is connected to the original fraud or has purchased the victim list — a reload scheme
The victim's bank leaked the information
c14_j2.e: Knowledge of the loss details is evidence of connection to the first fraud, not of authenticity — victim lists are a traded commodity and reload schemes exploit exactly this misplaced trust. Anyone contacting a victim already knowing the original fraud's specifics should be presumed connected to it.

c14_j3.t: Which statement about consumer fraud victims is MOST consistent with the research?
o: Only poorly educated consumers are victimised
Older victims tend to suffer higher losses per incident, while younger, more online-active consumers report fraud more frequently
Victimisation is evenly distributed across all demographics
The elderly are the most frequently victimised group across all scam categories
c14_j3.e: Frequency and severity are different measures. Older victims hold more assets and are targeted for larger sums (higher loss per incident); younger, digitally exposed consumers report incidents more often. An option asserting the elderly are the most frequently victimised conflates the two — a deliberate trap.

c14_d1.t: Scheme A demands an up-front 'processing fee' to release a lottery prize that does not exist. Scheme B contacts a prior scam victim offering, for a fee, to recover their lost money. These are, respectively:
o: An advance-fee scheme and a reload (recovery-room) scheme
A reload scheme and an advance-fee scheme
c14_d1.e: Demanding payment up front for a non-existent windfall is a classic advance-fee scheme. Targeting a known prior victim with a recovery offer is a reload scheme. Both take money up front, but reloading is defined by the victim having already been defrauded.

c14_d2.t: A scheme pays participants chiefly for enrolling others and requires each to buy stock they cannot resell. A separate business pays commissions on genuine retail sales to end consumers. These are, respectively:
o: An unlawful pyramid (inventory loading) and a lawful multi-level marketing business
A lawful MLM and an unlawful pyramid
c14_d2.e: Recruitment-driven compensation plus inventory loading (recruits forced to buy unsellable stock) marks the unlawful pyramid. Compensation from genuine retail sales to end users is lawful MLM. The product's existence is not the test; the source of the money is.

c14_s1.scenario: Over five months, an individual develops an online relationship with someone claiming to be an engineer working overseas. The correspondent is attentive and consistent, never able to video-call for plausible-sounding reasons. Eventually a crisis arises: equipment impounded by customs, requiring an urgent payment to release it, with a promise of swift repayment. The victim is asked to send funds by cryptocurrency and told not to mention it to family, who 'wouldn't understand'. After the first payment, further crises follow, each requiring more money.
c14_s1.t: The scheme and its defining structural feature are:
o: A reload scheme; the victim was previously defrauded
A pyramid scheme; recruitment of others
Romance/relational fraud; a cultivated relationship exploited through escalating manufactured crises with irrevocable payments and enforced secrecy
An advance-fee scheme; the fee is for a prize
c14_s1.e: A cultivated relationship followed by escalating manufactured crises, with irrevocable crypto payments and enforced secrecy from family, is romance/relational fraud — now among the highest-loss consumer frauds. No prize, no recruitment, and no prior fraud is described.

c14_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, why is the instruction to keep the payments from family a particularly significant indicator?
o: It shows the correspondent values privacy
It indicates the relationship is genuine
It suggests the funds are for a tax-sensitive purpose
Isolation removes the intervention most likely to stop the fraud, and serves no legitimate purpose
c14_s2.e: Enforced secrecy exists solely to prevent third-party intervention — a family member or bank teller is the most likely circuit-breaker. There is no legitimate reason for a genuine creditor or partner to require concealment from the victim's family, which is why this tactic recurs across nearly every consumer scam.

c15_d1.t: Debtor A omits a holiday property from the bankruptcy schedules. Debtor B spends five years building supplier credit, then triples orders, sells the goods below cost for cash, diverts the proceeds and files. These are, respectively:
o: Concealment of assets and a bust-out
A bust-out and concealment of assets
c15_d1.e: Omitting an existing asset from the schedules is concealment of assets — the most common bankruptcy fraud. Building credit then deliberately liquidating and defaulting is a bust-out — planned insolvency. One hides what exists; the other manufactures the collapse.

c15_j1.t: Which is the MOST COMMON form of bankruptcy fraud, and which is the most heavily tested?
o: Trustee embezzlement is most common; concealment most tested
Concealment of assets is most common; bust-out is most heavily tested
Petition mills are most common; multiple filings most tested
Bust-out is most common; concealment is most tested
c15_j1.e: Concealment of assets — omitting assets or transferring them pre-filing — is the most frequent bankruptcy fraud in practice. Bust-out is the scheme the exam tests most heavily. Both facts are worth holding separately.

c15_j2.t: In a bankruptcy, which party collects and liquidates estate assets and investigates the debtor's affairs?
c15_j2.e: The trustee administers the estate — collecting, liquidating, and investigating. An examiner is appointed where fraud is suspected and investigates only, without administering. The debtor in possession retains business control in a reorganisation, subject to fiduciary duties.

c15_j3.t: Which red flag points MOST directly to a planned bust-out rather than genuine business failure?
o: The business lost its largest customer
Credit purchases surged across many suppliers in one quarter, with goods sold below cost for cash shortly before filing
Margins declined steadily over three years
c15_j3.e: Genuine failure shows gradual deterioration. A sudden surge in credit orders followed by below-cost cash liquidation is the bust-out signature — no genuinely collapsing business buys more inventory than ever before and dumps it below cost. Declining margins, customer loss, and downturns are ordinary distress indicators.

c15_s1.scenario: An electronics distributor traded steadily for five years with modest, consistent ordering and a clean payment record. In a single quarter it tripled its purchases across eleven suppliers, all on 60-day terms, citing an anticipated contract. The goods moved out within weeks at roughly 60% of cost through a cash-only outlet with no prior relationship to the business. Two weeks after the final delivery, the company filed for bankruptcy. Bank records show corresponding deposits into accounts controlled by two directors. The anticipated contract never existed.
o: Genuine insolvency after a failed contract
A bust-out — planned insolvency exploiting built-up credit
c15_s1.e: Every bust-out element is present: five years spent building the credit that was then deliberately spent, a sudden multi-supplier surge on terms, below-cost cash liquidation, proceeds diverted to directors, and a fabricated justification. The credit history was the asset being liquidated. Genuine insolvency does not feature below-cost dumping with diverted proceeds.

c15_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, at which moment was the fraud most realistically detectable by the suppliers?
o: At the surge in credit orders — a tripling of volume across eleven suppliers, inconsistent with five years of history
When the goods were sold below cost
When the directors' bank deposits were traced
c15_s2.e: By the filing, the goods and money are gone. The credit surge is the detectable moment — a sudden tripling against five years of consistent ordering, replicated across eleven suppliers, is visible to any supplier running credit-limit reviews. The below-cost sales and bank tracing are only visible after the fact.

c16_d1.t: Taxpayer A uses a complex but fully disclosed structure that lawfully reduces liability. Taxpayer B maintains a second set of till records and omits cash sales. These are, respectively:
c16_d1.e: Full disclosure of a lawful structure = avoidance, however aggressive. A second set of books concealing cash sales = evasion — an affirmative act of concealment with wilfulness. The discriminator is legality and concealment, not complexity.

c16_j1.t: Which element most clearly separates criminal tax evasion from an honest reporting error?
o: Wilfulness — a voluntary, intentional violation of a known legal duty, evidenced by an affirmative act
Whether the taxpayer is an individual or a company
Whether a professional prepared the return
c16_j1.e: Wilfulness is the decisive element, and evasion further requires an affirmative act rather than mere omission. Negligence, genuine mistake, or good-faith misreading of a complex rule defeats it. Amount, preparer, and entity type are irrelevant to the distinction.

c16_j2.t: An examiner computes the change in a subject's assets less liabilities, adds living expenses, and subtracts known reported income to impute unreported income. Which method is this, and why is it used?
o: The expenditures method; because spending is always documented
Benford's Law; because digits reveal manipulation
The bank deposits method; because deposits are easiest to obtain
The net worth method; because direct evidence of unreported income is rarely available
