c16_j2.e: That formula is the net worth method, an indirect technique used precisely because direct proof of unreported income is rare. An unexplained rise in wealth plus living costs, less known legitimate sources, is income the taxpayer must explain — the arithmetic becomes the evidence.

c16_s1.scenario: A restaurateur declares annual income of 30,000. Over four years his net worth rises by 480,000: two properties purchased without mortgages, and school fees of 60,000 per year paid in cash. He received no inheritance, gift, or loan in the period. Investigators find a second set of till records at the premises recording daily takings substantially higher than those entered in the accounting system, and the difference approximates the unexplained wealth.
c16_s1.t: Which method establishes the unreported income, and which fact establishes wilfulness?
o: Expenditures method; the absence of a mortgage
Bank deposits method; the cash school fees
Benford's Law; the round-number property purchases
Net worth method; the maintenance of a second set of till records as an affirmative act of concealment
c16_s1.e: The net worth method imputes the income: wealth increase plus living expenses, less known reported sources. Wilfulness is established by the second set of till records — an affirmative act of concealment, not mere omission or carelessness. Both halves are needed: the arithmetic proves the income, the second books prove the intent.

c16_j3.t: A victim discovers a fraudulent refund was claimed in their name. How does this typically come to light?
o: The victim's own genuine return is rejected because a return already exists for that identity
The revenue authority telephones the victim
c16_j3.e: Stolen-identity refund fraud surfaces when the real taxpayer files and the system rejects it as a duplicate — the fraudster's entire advantage is filing first. Revenue authorities do not typically telephone, and employers and bureaus have no visibility of the filing.

c17_j1.t: An analyst compiles a competitor's public patent filings, job postings, regulatory filings and trade-show handouts, and deduces its unreleased product roadmap. Is this lawful, and why?
o: Yes — but only if the competitor consents
No — aggregating public data is prohibited
No — the conclusion was confidential, so it is espionage
Yes — lawful competitive intelligence, because the line is the method of collection, not the value of the conclusion
c17_j1.e: The distinction between intelligence and espionage is the method, not the sensitivity of what is deduced. Every source here was public and lawfully obtained; skilful aggregation into a valuable conclusion remains lawful competitive intelligence. Consent is not required to read public information.

c17_j2.t: A company sues a former employee over a 'secret' pricing formula that was stored on an open shared drive, never marked confidential, with no NDA in place. The trade-secret claim most likely fails on which element?
o: That the employee had authorised access
Reasonable measures taken by the owner to maintain secrecy
That pricing formulas cannot be trade secrets
c17_j2.e: The claim fails on reasonable protective measures — the third element. Value is irrelevant if the owner never protected the information. Authorised access does not defeat a claim where protections existed, and pricing formulas certainly can qualify when properly safeguarded.

c17_j3.t: An investigator examining a departed engineer suspected of taking designs should focus on which period, and why?
o: The final day of employment, when removal would occur
The engineer's probation period years earlier
The first month after joining the competitor
The 60–90 days preceding the resignation, where exfiltration typically shows as a ramp-up in bulk downloads, printing and after-hours access
c17_j3.e: Exfiltration almost always shows a ramp-up in the weeks before departure — bulk transfers, unusual printing, after-hours access. This is precisely why exit procedures that begin on the last day detect nothing; the evidence sits in the preceding quarter's logs.

c17_d1.t: Investigator A obtains a rival's data by telephoning its help desk posing as an IT contractor. Investigator B obtains equivalent insight from the rival's published regulatory filings. These are, respectively:
o: Espionage (via pretexting) and lawful competitive intelligence
c17_d1.e: Obtaining information through a false identity is pretexting — a deceptive method, hence espionage. Reading published filings is lawful competitive intelligence. Identical information; the method determines legality.

c17_s1.scenario: A speciality chemicals firm discovers that its lead formulation chemist resigned on a Friday and began work at a direct competitor the following Monday. IT logs show that over the preceding eleven weeks he transferred unusually large volumes of files to a personal cloud account outside working hours and printed the master formulation binder twice. The firm required all technical staff to sign NDAs, marked the formulations 'Confidential — Restricted', and limited access to a need-to-know list on which he appeared.
c17_s1.t: Assess the firm's trade-secret position and the evidentiary picture:
o: Weak — no physical property was removed
Strong — all three trade-secret elements are satisfied, and the pre-departure activity ramp evidences misappropriation
Weak — the chemist had authorised access, defeating any claim
Strong only if the competitor actually used the formulations
c17_s1.e: All three elements are met: economic value from secrecy, not readily ascertainable, and reasonable measures (NDAs, confidentiality marking, need-to-know access). Authorised access does not license misappropriation, no physical removal is required for digital exfiltration, and actual use by the competitor is not an element of the claim. The eleven-week ramp is the evidentiary spine.

c17_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which fact would MOST have weakened the firm's position had it been different?
o: If the competitor were in a different country
If the firm had never required NDAs, never marked the formulations confidential, and left access unrestricted
If the chemist had resigned with longer notice
If the transfers had occurred during working hours
c17_s2.e: Without NDAs, confidentiality marking, or access restriction, the third trade-secret element — reasonable measures — collapses, and there is no protectable trade secret however obvious the taking. Notice period, timing of transfers, and the competitor's location affect evidence or remedy, not the existence of the right.

c18_j1.t: Under accrual accounting, when is revenue properly recognised, and why does this matter to a fraud examiner?
o: When the invoice is issued, because that fixes the date
At the end of the fiscal year, for consistency
When it is earned regardless of cash timing — and almost all revenue fraud exploits the gap between earning and collection
When cash is received, because cash is objective
c18_j1.e: Accrual recognises revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, independent of cash. Nearly all revenue-recognition fraud lives in that gap — booking revenue before it is earned. Invoice issuance alone does not establish that revenue was earned, and year-end timing is irrelevant to recognition.

c18_j2.t: Which financial statement is generally the HARDEST for management to manipulate, and what follows for the examiner?
o: The statement of cash flows; so when earnings and operating cash flow persistently diverge, weight the cash flow
The statement of changes in equity; so trace dividends
The balance sheet; so verify assets first
The income statement; so recompute revenue
c18_j2.e: The statement of cash flows is hardest to manipulate — cash either arrived or it did not. That is precisely why a persistent divergence between reported earnings and operating cash flow is the strongest FSF signal, and why the examiner weights cash flow over accrual-based figures.

c18_j3.t: A fraudster inflates reported revenue. Because the accounting equation must balance, what necessarily follows, and how does the examiner exploit it?
o: An offsetting asset must be inflated (typically receivables) or a liability suppressed — so look for the implausible asset or missing liability
Nothing follows; revenue is independent of the balance sheet
Cash must increase by the same amount
c18_j3.e: Every entry balances, so inflated revenue forces an offsetting inflated asset (usually receivables) or a suppressed liability. That forced offset is the trail — which is why receivables ballooning faster than sales is such a reliable indicator. Cash need not increase (indeed, in fictitious revenue it does not).

c18_d1.t: Analyst A expresses every income-statement line as a percentage of sales for each of three years. Analyst B computes the percentage change in each line from year to year. These are, respectively:
c18_d1.e: Vertical (common-size) analysis states each line as a percent of a base within a period. Horizontal analysis measures change across periods. Vertical exposes an abnormal margin or COGS shift; horizontal exposes an abnormal growth rate.

c19_d1.t: Employee A sets up a company that invoices her employer for consulting never performed. Employee B sets up a company that genuinely buys components and resells them to the employer at a 40% markup, without disclosing her ownership. These are, respectively:
o: A pass-through scheme and a shell-company scheme
A shell-company scheme and a pass-through (turnaround) scheme
c19_d1.e: A shell bills for goods or services never delivered. A pass-through delivers real goods but at an inflated markup through an undisclosed intermediary. The common error is assuming a pass-through delivers nothing — it does deliver; the fraud is the markup and concealed ownership.

c19_d2.t: A cashier rings a sale, then processes a false refund and removes the cash. Another cashier takes cash from a sale and never rings it at all. These are, respectively:
o: A register disbursement scheme and skimming
c19_d2.e: A false refund is a recorded transaction created to justify removing cash = register disbursement (on-book). Taking cash with no entry at all = skimming (off-book). The discriminator is whether a fraudulent record was created — register disbursements leave one, skimming leaves none.

c19_j1.t: Which control is MOST effective at detecting a ghost-employee scheme?
o: Requiring two signatures on the payroll bank account
Periodically distributing paycheques in person and reconciling recipients to active HR records
c19_j1.e: In-person distribution reconciled to active HR records exposes ghosts directly — no real person appears to claim a fictitious employee's pay. Signature controls, encryption, and auditor rotation do nothing to reveal that a payee does not exist.

c19_j2.t: An examiner has time for one analytic across a year of accounts-payable data. Which combination is MOST likely to surface a billing scheme?
o: Duplicate-invoice testing, round-dollar detection, vendor-address matching against employee addresses, and clustering of invoices just below approval thresholds
c19_j2.e: Those four tests target the structural signatures of billing fraud: duplicates, artificial round amounts, vendors sharing an employee's address, and invoices deliberately sized just under an approval limit. Depreciation, bank balances, and dividends have no bearing on fraudulent vendor payments.

c19_j3.t: What makes cheque and payment tampering distinct from the other disbursement families?
o: It can only be committed by managers
The fraudster prepares or alters the payment instrument itself, rather than only falsifying supporting documentation
c19_j3.e: Tampering is unique because the fraudster physically prepares or alters the instrument — forging the maker's or payee's signature, or changing the payee or amount. The other families falsify supporting documents (invoices, timesheets, expense claims) to induce a legitimate-looking payment.

c19_s1.scenario: A construction firm's internal audit reviews payments to subcontractors. One vendor, registered eighteen months ago, has been paid 340,000 across 41 invoices. The vendor has no website, no telephone listing, and a registered address that matches the home address of a project manager's spouse. Every invoice was approved by that same project manager, each falls between 8,200 and 9,600 against a 10,000 approval threshold, and none is supported by a delivery note, site log entry, or inspection record. No site worker recalls the subcontractor attending.
c19_s1.t: The scheme and its two clearest structural signatures are:
o: Cheque tampering; forged maker and altered payee
Payroll fraud; ghost employees and inflated rates
Expense reimbursement fraud; mischaracterised and duplicate claims
A shell-company billing scheme; the vendor-address match to an employee's household and invoices deliberately clustered just below the approval threshold
c19_s1.e: A vendor with no operational footprint, an address matching an employee's household, invoices approved solely by that employee, no evidence of work performed, and amounts clustered just under the approval limit is a textbook shell-company billing scheme. The threshold clustering is deliberate structuring to avoid higher-level review. No instrument was altered, and no payroll or expense claim is involved.

c19_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which control failure most directly enabled the scheme?
o: The same individual could both select the vendor and approve its invoices, with no independent verification that work was performed
The approval threshold was set too high in absolute terms
Invoices were submitted on paper rather than electronically
The firm used subcontractors at all
c19_s2.e: The scheme required one person to control both vendor selection and invoice approval, with no independent confirmation of delivery — a segregation-of-duties failure. Threshold level is secondary (the fraudster simply sized invoices to fit); using subcontractors and paper invoices are normal business practices, not control failures.

c19_d3.t: Employee A buys a personal laptop and submits it on an expense report as 'client supplies'. Employee B submits the same genuine taxi receipt twice in two months. These are, respectively:
o: A mischaracterised expense and a duplicate reimbursement
An overstated expense and a fictitious expense
c19_d3.e: A genuine purchase that is personal but reported as business = mischaracterised expense (the most common variant). Submitting the same real receipt twice = duplicate reimbursement. Overstated inflates a real business cost; fictitious invents one that never occurred.

flashcards.a: Skimming = theft of cash BEFORE recording (off-book, no trail). Cash larceny = theft AFTER recording (on-book, creates a discrepancy).
Crediting one customer's account with a later customer's payment to conceal stolen receipts, rolling the shortfall forward. Classic receivables-skimming concealment.
Fictitious revenue, timing differences, concealed liabilities, improper disclosures, improper asset valuation.
Bribery = intent to INFLUENCE a future decision. Illegal gratuity = reward AFTER a decision, no prior agreement to influence.
Placement → Layering → Integration. (Structuring/smurfing is a placement technique.)
Financial statement fraud = least frequent, highest median loss. Asset misappropriation = most frequent, lowest median loss. Corruption in between.
Shell = bills for goods/services never delivered. Pass-through = actually buys goods then resells to employer at inflated markup.
Exploiting the float (clearing delay) between accounts/banks to create artificial balances from insufficient funds.
Ponzi = returns paid from new investors' money. Pyramid = income chiefly from recruitment, not product sales.
Evasion = illegal, willful intent to defeat tax. Avoidance = lawful minimization of tax.
Analyze data → create hypothesis (worst-case) → test hypothesis → refine. General to specific; least- to most-culpable.
Totality of circumstances leading a reasonable, trained professional to believe fraud occurred/is occurring/will occur. Required before any examination.
Beyond a reasonable doubt (criminal) > clear and convincing > preponderance of evidence ('more likely than not', civil).
Material false statement, knowledge of falsity, reliance by victim, resulting damages.
Direct proves a fact without inference (eyewitness). Circumstantial requires an inference (fingerprints). Fraud cases are mostly circumstantial — and that's valid.
Unbroken documented record of who held evidence and when. A gap can make evidence inadmissible.
A matching hash (MD5/SHA) proves a forensic image is bit-for-bit identical to the original and unaltered. Always work on the image, never the original.
Introductory → Informational → Closing → Assessment → Admission-seeking. Last two only when warranted.
Admission-seeking technique offering two incriminating choices, one more face-saving, to move the subject toward confession.
Asset increases + living expenses − income from known sources = likely illicit/unreported funds. Headline indirect tracing method.
Applies to natural numbers (invoice/payment amounts), NOT assigned numbers (phone, account, ID). Leading digit 1 ≈ 30.1%.
A fraud examiner must NOT opine on the legal guilt/innocence of the accused — that's for the trier of fact. Opine only within expertise.
Pressure + Opportunity + Rationalization (Cressey). The foundational fraud concept. Fraud Diamond adds Capability.
Asset misappropriation (most frequent, least costly) → Corruption → Financial statement fraud (least frequent, most costly).
Control environment, Risk assessment, Control activities, Information & communication, Monitoring activities.
Separate authorization, recording, and custody of assets. Its absence is the most-cited control weakness.
Management — not auditors. Management is primarily responsible for preventing/detecting fraud. Auditors give reasonable (not absolute) assurance.
Inherent = risk before controls. Residual = risk remaining after mitigating controls. Assess inherent first.
Tips. This is why reporting hotlines are among the most effective anti-fraud controls.
(1) Never opine on legal guilt/innocence. (2) Obtain evidence giving a reasonable basis for any opinion rendered.
The METHOD, not the value. Public sources = lawful intelligence. Deception, trespass, bribery, interception = espionage.

flashcards.q: Three elements of a trade secret?
flashcards.a: (1) Independent economic value from secrecy, (2) not readily ascertainable, (3) owner took REASONABLE MEASURES to protect it. Element 3 is where claims die.

flashcards.q: Synthetic identity theft — why so hard to detect?
flashcards.a: There is NO real victim to complain. Built from real fragments + fabricated details. Nurtured, then busted out.
Thief gives victim's name to police on arrest. Victim finds out via warrant or failed background check.
Large deposit offered to a bank ON CONDITION it makes a loan to a designated party. Deposit = bait, bad loan = payoff.
Conspirators pass an asset among themselves at escalating prices to inflate value before pledging it. Tell = velocity between related parties, no improvement to asset.
No property, no borrower, no collateral. Entirely fabricated file.
Take title, collect the rents, never service the mortgage, let it foreclose.
Profits derived predominantly from the EFFORTS OF OTHERS. If the investor's own labour drives the return, it is not a security.
Ponzi = passive investors paid from LATER INVESTORS' PRINCIPAL. Pyramid = investors paid for RECRUITING. Mechanism differs; both unsustainable.
Does the money come from RETAIL SALES to real end users (lawful) or from RECRUITMENT + inventory loading (unlawful pyramid)?
Broker over-trades a controlled account to generate commissions. Needs control + trading excessive for client's objectives.
Broker trades AHEAD of a large client order it knows is coming.
Forged MAKER = the DRAWER's signature is fake. Forged ENDORSEMENT = cheque genuinely signed, but the PAYEE's signature is fake.
Average daily FLOAT greatly exceeds average LEDGER BALANCE. Matched cheques between 2+ banks against uncollected funds.
Build a good payment record to raise limits → max every line → disappear. The good history IS the investment phase.
A complicit merchant runs another (unauthorised) merchant's card transactions through its own account for a fee.
NO — PSEUDONYMOUS. Blockchain is a permanent public ledger. Investigative leverage is at the exchange on/off ramps (KYC).
Agent collects premium and never remits it to the insurer. Most common agent fraud — discovered only at claim time.
CHURNING = replace policy within SAME insurer for commission. TWISTING = misrepresent to induce switch to ANOTHER insurer. SLIDING = charge for coverage client never agreed to.
Owner arranges the theft/destruction of their OWN insured vehicle to claim proceeds.

flashcards.q: Workers' comp PREMIUM fraud — who commits it?
flashcards.a: The EMPLOYER. Understates payroll, misclassifies workers into low-risk codes, misstates claims history to cut premium.
UPCODING = bill a HIGHER-LEVEL service than performed. UNBUNDLING = bill SEPARATELY for parts of one bundled procedure.
Referring a patient among practitioners in the same clinic so each can bill, without clinical need.
Institutional upcoding — systematically coding admissions into higher-reimbursing diagnosis groups.

flashcards.q: Why is waiving patient co-pays a red flag?
flashcards.a: It removes the patient's only price signal and acts as an inducement to accept unnecessary services.
Returning to an ALREADY-DEFRAUDED victim for a second bite (often as a 'recovery service'). Knowing the loss details = evidence of CONNECTION, not legitimacy.
Build credit → order huge inventory on credit → sell below cost for cash → divert proceeds → file bankruptcy. Detectable moment = the SURGE, not the failure.
CONCEALMENT OF ASSETS (omitting from schedules, transferring to relatives/shells). Bust-out is the most TESTED, but concealment is the most FREQUENT.
AVOIDANCE = lawful arrangement. EVASION = unlawful concealment. Evasion needs: tax due + AFFIRMATIVE ACT + WILFULNESS.
(Assets − Liabilities) change + living expenses − known reported income = imputed unreported income. Indirect method; used when direct evidence is unavailable.
VIRUS needs a host file AND user action. WORM needs NEITHER — self-replicating, self-propagating. Overnight network-wide spread = worm.
Dormant code triggered by a CONDITION (a date, or the author's payroll record vanishing). Classic disgruntled-privileged-insider weapon.
AVAILABILITY. It denies service. It does NOT exfiltrate data. Beware options saying 'steals data by flooding the server'.
Slicing tiny amounts (rounding fractions) from many accounts. Individually invisible, collectively large.

flashcards.q: Bid tailoring vs bid rigging — WHEN?
flashcards.a: TAILORING = PRESOLICITATION phase (specs written for one vendor). RIGGING = SOLICITATION/EVALUATION phase. The exam distinguishes by WHEN.
COMPLEMENTARY (cover bids to fake competition — most common), ROTATION (take turns winning), SUPPRESSION (agree not to bid), MARKET DIVISION (carve up territories).
Abnormally LOW winning bid + abnormally HIGH volume of change orders. The low bid was never the real price.
SUBSTITUTION = deliver lower-grade goods, bill for specified grade. DEFECTIVE PRICING = submit cost/pricing data that isn't current, accurate, complete.

flashcards.q: Conflict of interest — is a payment needed?
flashcards.a: NO. The UNDISCLOSED INTEREST is itself the violation. No bribe, no loss, no unfair price required.
FREQUENCY: asset misappropriation > corruption > financial statement fraud. MEDIAN LOSS: exactly REVERSED. The commonest is cheapest; the rarest is dearest.

flashcards.q: Fraud triangle — which element can the org control?
flashcards.a: OPPORTUNITY. Pressure and rationalisation live in the fraudster's head; internal controls attack opportunity.
CASH RECEIPTS: off-book theft BEFORE recording (no trail). IDENTITY THEFT: a card-data capture DEVICE. Unrelated schemes, same word.
100 questions / 2h45m = ~100 seconds each. Open-book is a SAFETY NET for a handful of flagged items, not a research strategy.
